p.s: There was a certain man very prosperous in the land of the Arabians, called Ausitis long ago, a food of the field.
There a certain man dwelt in a house, both good and great, and his famous and far-renowned name was Job.
Who revered justice, since his mind was god-fearing, and he turned aside from evil, and guarded all things that are right.
To this man also ten children were born in his halls: seven were sons, and three were fair-haired daughters.

He had countless cattle, and high-ridged camels — three thousand females with young, pastured for him on the mountains — and seven thousand sheep, and again fifty yoke of broad-browed oxen, and fifty donkeys, and many possessions.
For truly his livelihood was beyond telling.
Not for any men, heroes, who were the most blessed and dwelt at the risings of the shining Sun, was there so great a number.
And his sons feasted on countless meats and sweet wine.
Each day in turn, in his own house, each feasted, and by three he called his brothers to the feast.
Thus they all day long (for they had abundance) welcomed one another, and feasted in the halls, drinking and eating, taking turns among their houses.

But when the fair-tressed Dawn had brought to fulfillment all the days of the honey-sweet feast, and the seasons had turned round about, straightway he, as a father purifies his banqueting sons, all according to due order, and at the same time as the morning appeared he would offer sacrifices and choice hecatombs to the Immortal, in case anyone had overstepped and sinned, or spoken evil of God with the tongue's folly of his mind.
As many children as he had, so many fair sacrifices would he offer.
Thus he would do continually throughout.
For he himself knows what kinds of transgressions young men's deeds become.
For swifter is the mind, and subtle is the counsel in all deeds, but most of all in the hour of the feast.
For wine sets even a very prudent man to singing, and it sends forth some word which is better left unspoken.
And there was a day when the Angels came before God.

And they stood beside their Father in a throng, and among them came Satan too, weaving deadly counsels in his mind — the wretch, the mighty worker, who perished not though he did lawless deeds — lion-hearted, grim, a wrought evil for mankind.
And when the Father of men and gods perceived him, then he addressed him, spoke a word, and called him out: "O Satan, whence do you come?"
But the man-hater answered: 'Having wandered much and greatly, and having traveled over the whole earth, wandering much and being much astray, I have come.'
And the Father in turn addressed him and questioned him with a word: 'Wretch, did you ever notice my servant Job?'
Who is dearest to me, and I honor him as surpassing others, since surely no one of earth-dwelling men is like him.
He who accomplished justice, since his mind is god-fearing, turned away from evil, and guarded all things that are ordained.
Answering him, the crafty Demon spoke, the destroyer Satan, who knows baneful counsels: Is it then in vain and for nothing that Job reveres God?
Did you not set a fence around his well-shaded house on every side, and around his possessions, and around that man himself?
By your kindly dispositions his works flow fair, and his prosperity and wealth increase in the land.
But come now, touch his possessions a little, and then, blundering in speech, he will greatly outrage you to your face, mocking, and looking you in the eye he will speak with shameful words.
So he spoke;
the liar, trusting in his own chosen wits.
And answering him, God of the crooked counsel spoke: Now, look, all that he had has been turned over into your hands;
But only keep your own heavy hands off him.
So then the Father spoke, and laid a mighty word upon him.
Satan went out to be there, and in his mind he devised evil deeds.
While Job's sons and daughters together, all of them in the halls of their eldest brother, were feasting, and their heart lacked nothing of the equal feast;
On that day a certain wretched messenger came to Job, shedding hot tears, and he spoke with a grievous message:
While the oxen were being yoked, and the donkeys grazing nearby, the Sabeans rushed upon them and carried them off, and they killed the plowmen with the sharp bronze;
I alone escaped, and I came to you as a wretched messenger.

Not yet had the whole word been spoken, when another messenger stood in the doorways, saying that a fire sent from God, coming down from heaven, had utterly burned up both the sheep and the shepherds themselves, with the baleful fury of the thunderer;
I alone escaped, and I came to you as a grievous messenger.

Not yet had the whole word been spoken, when another came in, bursting into tears, and lamenting he spoke a word: the Chaldeans drew up their ranks in three divisions, and swiftly rushing in they carried off the camels, and again they slew the servants, the herdsmen, with the sharp bronze.
I alone escaped, and I came to you as a grievous messenger.
Not yet had the whole word been spoken, when Fourth stood near (for always evil was joined to evil;

As when the long waves of the sea are poured one upon another in quick succession, first one and then another) He shed hot tears, and spoke a lamenting word: Ah me, blameless Job, nurtured of Zeus, surely you shall hear of a grievous message, which ought never to have come to be.
For as long as your sons and well-girded daughters were seated in the halls of their eldest brother, delighting their dear heart with food and wine—
Then at that moment a fierce storm-wind of the wind came rushing in and, darting from the desert, struck the great high-roofed house;
And the force of the wind shattered its joints and sides from the foundation;
and it fell upon the young men, and they perished;
I alone escaped, and I came to you as a grievous messenger.
So he spoke.
And a black cloud of grief covered him.
He sprang up with a wail, and tore his great purple mantle about his breast, and sheared off his dear hair, and fell down in the dust like one breathing his last.
For a long while speechlessness at words seized him, and his two eyes were filled with tears, and his voice was held back, abundant.
At last, having breathed again, he began a vehement lament, and at the same time, mourning, he spoke a god-fearing word.
Ah, woe is me, wretched man!
A mother bore me naked.
And she brought me forth into the light, and I saw the rays of the sun;
And naked I shall go back again beneath the belly of the earth.
God gave, and He took away, since His might is greatest;
Therefore may His glorious name be blessed forever.
Thus he spoke in piety, and he did not err in his words, nor did he reproach God with the follies of his mind.
And again there was a day when all the Angels came together before the Immortal One, and they gathered together, and Satan was with them too, brooding on evil in his heart.
And the Father questioned him, and shook great Olympus;
O Satan, from where have you come, you wretch?
And what is your business?
And he, the man-hater, answered him with guile: 'I have wandered much, and I have traveled over the whole earth, and I have seen the cities of many men, and I have come to know their mind;'
But now I also come to the sacred city of the immortals.
Then the Olympian addressed him again in a stormy voice: 'Do you know that, wandering much through the cities, you have come here?'
But come, tell me this, and recount accurately: did you, having observed, see my clear blameless man Job?

He who honors me most of men that walk upon the earth, and shuns transgression, and knows in his heart what is right, and clings fast to righteousness, though grieving, and suffers grievous pains through your evil plots.
Then the crafty-minded Demon, the destroyer Satan, who knows baneful counsels, answered him with a taunt:
Skin for skin, and all that a man has — know that he will give countless things; a man will give his life-ransom.

But if, while he is still alive, you should openly scrape his wound, and even if you should strike his flesh and bones with a glancing blow, then Dalerophres will suddenly appear speaking otherwise, and will revile you openly with angry words.
And answering him, God of the crooked counsel spoke: 'Look, Nis, under your hands I have turned him and him himself.'
And another thing I will tell you, and do you lay it up in your mind.
Do not speak of death, since I think I could still persuade you.
For it is not yet his lot to die and meet his doom.
So then the Father spoke, and laid upon him a mighty word.
Satan went to go, and devised evils in his heart against Job.
With scabby plagues and dread sores he was from head to feet.
and his skin wasted away upon his bones.
And thick scabs ran up and down along his sides and shoulders, blood-red.
And he himself kept scraping his moist skin with a potsherd; he had not scratched with his teeth, and he sat in the dust, wiping his grievous sores, wiping away much toil.
And his wife too assailed him with reproachful words:
Ah, wretched among men, most miserable of all mortals, fool, in piety and righteousness vain — how long will you hold on thus in vain?
since there is no need of anything for you.
Surely now would your virtue and fear of God avail you?
Or did your piety ward off grievous destruction?
But come, blaspheme, and die!
Why do you still linger?
Better either to perish once and for all, or to live, than to be worn away long in painful misery.
But the noble husband, greatly angered, answered her, ever keeping in his breast a grief-enduring spirit: 'Foolish woman, what word has escaped the fence of your teeth?'
O woman, how foolishly you hold it in your heart, or are you babbling these things?
You are dull and foolish, since you have not spoken according to what is right.
Shall we receive good things only from God, and never evil things?
He who gives both good and evil;
for he is able to do all things.
For two jars lie stored in the seat of God, such as he gives of gifts:
of evils, and another of good things.
Ah, whichever God of shifting counsel may give him mingled, at one time he meets with evil, at another with good.
Ah, and if he may give of those grievous things, he has made him a thing of outrage, and a vile devouring drives him over the shining earth.
So he spoke rebuking, nor did he sin in what he said, nor yielding to folly did he babble idle words.

But when these things were being reported to the three friends of steadfast-hearted Job — for late a swift evil, a winged messenger, came to them — the noble companion suffered in the grave; and rising up they went down, each from his own house.
First was Eliphaz the Temanite, leader of men; second again was Bildad, pre-eminent among the Shuhites over others; and third was Zophar, a great hero among the Naamathites.
For they agreed to go as friends, grieving, both to lament together in their hearts and to be comforted with gentle words.
And good comfort is for a companion, for all men, but especially for those who grieve.
And they gazed at him from afar, and did not recognize him when they saw him.
And they wept shrilly, and each tore his cloak, and taking with both hands the sooty dust, he poured it on his head, and defiled his lovely face.
Thus for seven nights and days continuously, always sitting on the ground, they wailed shrilly around their comrade, and for a while they were unwilling to speak a word, nor to ask questions.
For their spirit in their breasts was stunned at the wretched man, when they saw the unbearable suffering and the grief...
For a long time they all sat silent with a grieving heart;
But at last noble, much-enduring Job spoke up, groaning very deeply, and loathing the day of his birth;
He cursed much;
for a mighty grief compelled him;
Lamenting piteously, he uttered his speech with wailing;
Let the wretched day perish in which my mother bore me;
And the night, when a messenger brought my father the ill-tidings and said, 'Hail to me, dear father,' — his wife escaped her birth-pangs, and to you a male child fell thus at a woman's feet.
So he spoke, bringing the news.
Would that the broad earth had gaped open for him.
Let darkness and gloom be that day, a lightless day.
Let God above not care for it, and let it be reckoned as nothing, so that it never have the sweet light of the sun, but the shadow of death and murky mist.
Let it be forever covered with mist and cloud, as a hateful, evil day, unutterable, not to be named, dreadful and dark, blacker than pitch.
And let Cimmerian darkness take hold of that night; let it perish from the months of the year, and let it not be counted among them.
Yes, that night is evil, horrible, moonless-dark, and barren.
And let no one hear a pleasant voice in it.
May those who curse this day, who are ready to rouse up mourning and unceasing lament, curse it as an evil and cruel day, and along with it the destructive black night.
May the evening stars of that night be lightless, may it have neither bright light nor gleaming moon.
May it never see the dawn, nor the dawn that gladdens mortals.
Because it did not shut the doors of my mother's womb, nor did it keep unceasing grief from my eyes.
Why did I not become a grave for myself, wretched as I am, within the womb?
I came forth from the womb;
would that I had perished right there.
Woe to me, my mother, why then did you nurse me to bear dreadful things?
Why did you cast me out, since you bore an ill-fated son?
Why then did an ill-named midwife, taking me in her divine arms, forestall me, newborn and still breathing from birth?
Away, thrice-wretched midwife of painful birth!
Why did a breast suckle me, an infant, and nurse me when I was tiny?

O that I had perished on that day when my mother first bore me, when an evil storm-blast of wind, carrying me off, had borne me to a mountain, or to a wave of the much-resounding sea, where the wave would have swept me away before these deeds came to be.
Now I would lie fearless in the soft bosom of the earth, safely and quietly, and I would sleep.
Where countless tribes of Zeus-nurtured kings lie alike, and leaders and rulers of peoples, and counselors of men sleep a sweet sleep;
For whom once fair dwellings, far from the throng of evils, golden, gleaming, have been built, imperishable forever.
Where the greatly-renowned lords lie down, who honored gold and heaped up silver, and wealth abundant and boundless in their houses.
O that I had been, as it were, a miscarriage, utterly swift-fated, or like a babe untimely born, which never yet has seen the light.
There at least those who devour their own heart cease from strife and are at rest.
And under grievous toil their dear limbs had been loosed; finding a respite, they breathe again from their labor.
And there the harsh bond used to subdue them together even in prison; quietly they lay there, having escaped their unbreakable fetters, and never did they hear the mighty rebuke of the oppressor.
There at least all are together, both small and great, mingled with one another, and sharers of an equal lot.
No longer does any servant, mindful of his glorious lord, escape the dread Erebus and the day of slavery; for they are equal shades, the lord and he who is in the lot of the hand.
An equal portion belongs to the ruler, even if one was born a very slave.
Why do they see the light, and why does it still come to the living — men wretched and having a carefree heart?
As when someone eagerly searches for a hidden treasure, eager to dig, seeking where he might find it;
As they wish to die and to follow their fate, longing that somehow they might be able to cut off death;
But they still live, yearning for destruction.
Such a welcome end of death covers them, and it is a joyful thing;
Greatly would they rejoice in their heart, as they come upon and obtain a share of sweet rest and the grave.
Why is light, and life, given to the ill-fated man, who under grief wanders hither and thither, and does not see where he might go, because God has shut him in with a dark, unseen cloud?
Woe is me, wretched man, why then should the greatest things happen to me?
Woe is me, because before eating, with groaning and wailing, grieving in my heart, I devour my own food;
From me, then, both Cocytus and wailing have been poured out, as from a spring, which down a sheer-cliffed rock pours murky water.
I suffer, all-wretched, because in my heart I fear exceedingly;
But this has now come upon me, which I long feared very much.
For I also said, before the fated day came on, that I would fill up sorrows;
and now all these things are being fulfilled.
For I was not yet free from care, though I had long been prospering, nor was my mind ever fearless amid feasts, nor was I without dread, but my heart was always foreseeing evil.
But now, contrary to my hope, grievous misery has come upon me.
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said to him:
If we venture to speak, will you not be angered?
Who could keep silent and restrain his tongue, when you are one whose words are many and disorderly, and you would heal them?
For the word is heart-biting, and you have urged me to speak.
And you were once a teacher of others, and into many men you have instilled noble strength;
Was it by your own wise understanding, and having gathered your spirit into your heart,
and with feeble hands you put strength and might?
And him who, already faint, was about to fall, you quickly made stand firm again by your words, and you were a support under his feet;
and on weak knees you set a stay and a defense.
But now that evil has come upon you, and it has touched you a little,
Nor are you able to endure, though you are a clear-voiced speaker;
But your own spirit was stirred within your breast, and your strength is loosed, and your heart within you barks.
Wretch, where indeed has your might gone, which you once had?
Is there no god-fearing mind in you, in which you trusted — piety, and courage, and righteousness, and hope?
But come now, if you know anything of the glorious deeds of men of old, having learned the works of former ages—
Of these now remind me, and tell me truly—
Who, being noble, has faith?
Or where has a righteous man perished?
What doom befell a man of upright mind?
if you could tell of that man's wretched destruction, if indeed you have seen it with your own eyes, or heard the report of another.
As I too have perceived, and have seen with my eyes: whatever sort a man is, such is the harvest that befalls him.
Those who plow a wicked thing, having likewise reaped a wicked thing, and sowing Ruin, they carried off a fitting wage, and a fruit equal to their sowing, reckless men, for what they did.
They are destroyed, then, when God is greatly angered — when God is angered — blown as by a bitter wind; from his nostrils a blast rushes out, and they perish.
By the dreadful roar of a roaring lion it was quenched, and the sound of the loud-bellowing lioness;
The jaws of the cubs, and the strong teeth were broken.
With grievous hunger the fair-maned lion perishes, the hunter, and the cubs of mighty lions were scattered.
Secretly, as a thief, a hidden word came to me as a messenger, when he had spoken a little; and my ears received the voice.
The dark night, when other mortals sleep, and the gates of the unspeakable dreams are spread open, and where many phantoms come upon the heads of men — then indeed a divine dream came to me in sleep.
As I saw, so I shuddered with fear from the dread thing, and trembling poured around me, and trembling seized my limbs.
And a spirit came near to me, standing by my head.
And the hairs stood upright on my shuddering limbs;
as I trembled;
for pale fear seized me greatly.

It stood still, and I could not yet discern its form face to face, but I beheld a dim phantom with my eyes, and while it spoke, a faint whisper came to me, and it said to me a word: Surely a man is not more righteous than God?
Or shall a mortal be more righteous than the Immortal, who made him and formed him when he was nothing?
Nor does he at all trust even his heavenly servants in his mind, who are always his attendants.
And he perceived folly even in his holy minds, who are his angels and diligent servants.
How is it not so among mortals?

(since never is the race of heavenly beings and of men who walk on the earth alike to think of) those who have houses of clay, founded on sand, Ablēchros, of no account, which the dappled worms eat, and also moths;
For to them it is destined that they become a sport.
In the morning they spring up, and in the evening they wither utterly, and no one of those perishing takes thought for them.
And their glory perished together with them, and these very men perished headlong miserably through their own follies.
But come now, call out, so that someone may hear your voice.
But to which of the holy ones will you turn, looking upon them, and make your plea?
So that in justice an advocate may stand near you?
On a fool a dread wrath sent an unseemly doom, and sharp indignation slew the light-minded man.
I saw a fool flourishing like a fair oak, firmly fixed with great roots;
But he perished at once, and all his grace withered away, and ruin seized his house, and the prosperous stranger too.
His children are not safe, and no light shines on them any more;
They are crushed in the gates, and there is no escape any more;
For there is no one present to help, who might ward off their fates.

Their wealth is eaten up, and their toilsome works have perished; and they eat the unharvested crop of their field, and the fruit of the soil, those whom famine once drove, even from amid thorns, greedily; and a thief ravages their possessions in their houses.
For trouble does not come from the earth, nor does ruin arise from the dust, nor does it spring up from the ground; it is not from the ancient oak, nor from the rock.
Just as sparks, slender (for such is the lot of the light), are kindled into a blazing, far-famed firebrand, and lightly indeed they fly on high, and are mingled in the clouds;
Thus man is born for toil, and for misery;
So that he should endure, ever groaning and suffering countless sorrows, and having suffered very many things and toiled much, to fill up the dread doom of his life;
For as fate spun for Teinomoros with the linen thread, when his mother bore him.

But if such grief, and the implacable fate, came upon me as now has subdued you by the will of the great God, then I would entreat him, and call upon the Most High, and I would wish to pray continually, nor at all yielding in folly to speak great things, but rather to entrust the whole matter to him.
since he is far mightier.
He who shows encompassing deeds, extraordinary signs, and very many untraceable, unseen wonders he works.
From on high, out of the clouds, he sent fruit-nourishing rain;
He sent rain upon the earth, and poured waters down to the ground; often he raised up the lowly, and made the obscure grow;
To the afflicted he granted that they be safe, and not to perish.
He scattered the snares of the crafty, and confounded their arts;
A deed, whatever they devise, shall not be accomplished.
He catches the wise in their own craftiness, and overturns the crooked counsels of the deceitful;
And they themselves perished by their own evil devices.
And they, even in the daytime, meet with hateful darkness, and grope with their hands at midday, as in the night.
But he saved the poor man from the sword and from battle, from the mighty mouth, and from the hand of the proud man.
So the poor man has hope, and is more confident, having once ceased from joyless misery;
But the sinners became voiceless from the mouth of the one who frightens them, in silence.
Thrice blessed is the man, and four times, whom God still gently chastises with bittersweet blows;
Therefore do not despise the chastening of your dear God.
He himself sends pain and healing; with his own hands he gives grievous wounds, and sprinkles soothing remedies.
He himself will rescue you with his right hand in six troubles; indeed not even in seven shall evil come near you.
Never at any time will you be frightened in war, nor in famine;
But in both of these you will escape death and doom, until God draws you away from missiles, and from dust, and from slaughter of men, and from blood, and from the din of battle.
No one will overpower you with the shrill whip of the tongue, until the slander-loving man attacks with abuse;
nor will you greatly be terrified in your heart at the onset of destruction.
You will laugh at destruction and famine, and from the untamed beasts, at plague and hunger, and you will not fear evil wild beasts.
For your stones will be in the crossroads, and in the mountains the beasts will be gentle, having dear counsels in your mind.
They will make agreements, and oaths of covenants.
You will know your peace, and much prosperity, of which you will see your house full, never erring.
Your dear child will be beyond measure, like grass that has grown in a meadow, exceedingly abundant.
Late you will go down to the grave, and in extreme old age you will come to the tomb, and you will be burned toward death, full of days.
As when in the summer season, having harvested the deep grain-field, they bring the tawny fruit to the well-wheeled threshing floors, and the wagons, pressed down by this, are weighed down greatly.
Handfuls of ears of grain, and the ears are filled with kernels.
These things we know clearly, how it stands;
But do you quickly understand all this for good, and lay it up in your heart.

Then noble Job, groaning heavily, answered him: 'Would that you would well weigh the burden of me who am burdened, and that grievous Ruin together on the scale were placed, and misery too in equal-balanced talents — all that I, wretched, have now toiled with enduring heart!'
All this, truly.
Nor would a hundred-benched ship carry the burden.
Nor would even the weight of the deep sand be so great, which is poured abundantly on the shore of the sea; therefore a different word escaped me, whatever I might say.
For in me the winged arrows of God were fixed;
And the deadly poison of the bitter arrows drank my blood and my life, and at once devoured all my inward parts.
Does the sluggish wild ass bray under famine as it grazes in the meadow? And does the ox bellow at the Pierian manger, feeding on white barley and spelt?
Could one eat something tasteless without salt?
Or is there thus any flavor in the throat, or in the white-of-egg words?
Whatever my soul, loathing them, refused to touch, these things my table has served me as a joyless feast.
Ah, wretch that I am, why should I wait after suffering dreadful things?
Would that it had been granted to me by the Immortal to fulfill this long-desired wish, which I have long yearned for and have long been awaiting;
As it might ever be dear to him to take away my life, so that striking me with his hand he might deprive me of hateful life.
And then there might be some comfort and respite from evil, and I would endure even though grieving, by necessity.
Would that my eyes might look past me, since I have not hidden a word from my breast, and all the oracles I have made clear.
But what strength have I?
What end shall be mine?
That I might endure, and still be among the living?
Am I stone-hearted?
And is my strength like rocks?
Am I like the strength of a rock, or a thread to blazing iron?
Is my frame adamant, and my flesh unyielding bronze?
Whence is my help?
Do I not myself have my help within?
Or has a god utterly destroyed my mind?
Always does the good man weave a compassionate purpose, and he cares for grieving friends, and he pities the wretched, if ever he fears any wrath of God.
But me, weighed down in mind by so many toils—
My brothers and companions deceived me with words.
And they came alongside, like a winter torrent flowing swiftly;
Easily they slipped away from me, just like the streams of a river;
On them, at least, smooth ice was frozen over on top, and snow, while beneath it nourished a dark wave, as before;
for it had been frozen solid by a brief frost;
But when the light of the sun and warmth come, then those warm things flow away, each in a different direction.
Their path is turned aside and becomes crooked, roaring;
Those things quickly grow dim, and they waste away utterly, and every river is dried up, and the bright water is poured out.
The Temanites saw it, and the Sabeans wait for it, until those drinking the much-parching thirst let it go.
But when they reached the deceitful streams of rivers, hope perished for them as the stream withered away;
As they saw, so shame and modesty seized them;
For it is shameful to wait long, and to return empty.
So you are treacherous, and cruel, and grievous, O wretches, base reproaches, watching my misery;
Why do you fear in this way and dread in your hearts?
Why do you stand thus astonished like fawns?

Did I ever say to you, 'Give me a good treasure, and bring me gifts on my behalf, friends, a ransom to my enemies; rescue me from the hands of hostile men, and from violent men who devise reckless things'?

lg.l: Δυσμενέων ἀνδρῶν ῥύσασθέ με ἐκ παλαμάων,
Ἔκ θ’ ὑβριστήρων ὃι ἀτάσθαλα μηχανόωνται;

p.s: Speak, and I will be silent.
Instruct me, whatever you know beforehand; but I, who would keep silent, will endure, having a listening ear, and I will not speak again, though my heart is greatly grieved.
Show me my transgressions, so that I may learn.
How forceful are upright words, from one who knows well in his mind!
And there is no little strength in words, when he has spoken according to what is right, and the encouragement of a comrade is good.
But why does your censure and blame now reprove me?
Fools, did you really claim to be censors of words, of a man beyond hope, whose words are like the winds?
For such as is the whispering of a shrill-breathing wind, such was the speech of a strengthless, cowardly man.
But your heart is unyielding, like an axe.
On an orphan child you have cast a grievous doom, and for a wretched companion you have dug a treacherous pit.
Hear me, friends, though I suffer evils.
Hold, friends, and leave me alone, then, of my guardians.
Look upon my ruin, and see me, what I have suffered;
For you know well (since you are not foolish) whether I speak truly, or not.
But turn back, friends, since it is not unfitting; but turn back, having a changed heart, considering my justice, since I am blameless.
Is there indeed on my tongue a grievous offense?
Or does a confused speech flow from my mouth?
Is it not, then, a destined day that has been sent to mortals?
Is there not a limit of life, and have the fates spun it out?
Him I say no one of men has yet escaped being?
Neither evil nor yet good, once these first things come to be.
And the days of men are as the days of a hired laborer.
As a shadow cheers a slave whose spirit is gasping, in the summer season, when he is terribly faint with toil, worn out by sweat under the heat;
As when a servant, with a steadfast heart, waits through nights and days, until he may receive his wage;
for that is the reward of those who toil;
and so a welcome end of toil has appeared for him.
So it is decreed for me to drag out a long time in vain, and months in endless toil.
Always I am held by grievous pain, and there is no way to breathe free of misery and wretched toil;
Nor did the sun ever see me at rest, nor the moon; but I groan by day, and I pass sleepless nights.
I lie on my bed awaiting the bright dawn;
When shall I arise?
I said, and, 'How long will the night still remain?'
All night long I keep awake, and I toss hither and thither, now lying on my sides, now again on my back, and now prone, grieved at heart.
Worms and clods of earth have covered my flesh all around, my skin is torn apart, gashed with wounds, defiled with blood and gore, all over my limbs.
It melts away relentlessly, and the whole body swells with grievous sores.
My life has perished without hope.
My life has gone swifter than a weaver's shuttle, which by the weaver's skill, swiftly brushing aside the thread, draws it on as it breathes.
Truly, do you not remember that my life darts swiftly like a storm, and of the unharvested aether, and I shall never again see good with my eyes?
No longer would an eye that once saw me look upon me again;
Your eyes are upon me, and I shall no longer endure for long.

For like a cloud, when the winds come upon it, stretched out by shrill blasts, it suddenly was gone; for the might of the wind swiftly scattered it with a wondrous tempest, and swept it away from Olympus.
So he who once has gone down into the house of Hades, would not come up again, since there is no return any more.
He could not return again to his house;
His place will no longer see him again, nor his homeland any more.
Therefore does the fence of my teeth not hold back my tongue?
Nor shall I keep silent;
My spirit bids me lament piteously because of grievous woes, and to gladden my dear heart with abundant wailing.

Am I then a sea, or a wild sea-monster in the swell of the deep, such as the brine has reared many monstrous ones, that you now bind me with fetters, casting bonds all around, and shut me in unshaken, so that they may never be escaped?

If ever I said, "That a bed will be a comfort to me, and a soft couch will stop my groaning" (for indeed that one was poured out in quiet, and sister to the grave), then meanwhile the evil spirit kept rushing dreams upon me, troubling me with nightly phantoms and visions.

lg.l: Τόφρα δ' ἐμοὶ κ' ὀνείρατ' ἐπέσσευεν κακὰ δαίμων,
Φάσμασι νυκτερινοῖσι καὶ ὀπτασίῃσι ταράσσων.

p.s: Therefore my soul desires choking, and my heart no longer wished to live, and to see the light of the sun.
Woe is me, what shall I suffer?
Since I would not wish to live forever and ever;
how I am burdened?
But leave me alone, O Father, O King, for my life is vanity.
For what is man, that you have stretched out glory to him?
Or is it that he has become so pleasing to your heart?
And do you stretch a watchful eye upon him all the day, and do you test him continually every hour?
How long will you not let me be safe?
Yet a little while, and will you not, until you have swallowed down my spittle from my throat?
I have sinned;
but what shall I do to you, O most exalted Savior of the race of man?
and why have you made me a mark, at which you would shoot aiming with arrows, so that I become to myself a most grievous burden?
Why then will you not rather let go my transgressions?
Why will you destroy me for my sin?
Soon I shall lie in the dust;
at dawn you will seek me, but I shall no longer be.
Meanwhile Bildad the Shuhite answered in reply, taunting Job with reproachful words:
How long will you speak these windy things idly and to no purpose?
How long will you babble in vain like this?
But your speech is as when shrill-blowing winds roar, which through the groves send forth a man's unpleasing hum?
Does the Almighty pervert upright justice?
Or did he judge crooked judgments among men?
If perhaps your infant children sinned against God, they perished by their own transgressions.
If you would seek God among the first, and with gentle prayers the ancestral one would be entreated.

If you were pure, and knowing your blameless house, the High-Ruler Lord would ever keep a wakeful watch over you, propitious, and standing by would guard, for the sake of your impiety, both your wife and your high-roofed house.
If you are small at first, yet later you shall be great; from a little beginning you shall be brought to perfection as you grow.
For inquire first about your generation, and search out both your fathers and the tribes of men born long ago.
Inquire thoroughly into all things, and the race of ancient men (for we are but yesterday's creatures on the earth, tribes of men, knowing nothing).
For whom life is as a shadow, life is as a shadow, and their life a dim phantom.
Will they not teach you, and will those men tell you, speaking fitting things with a knowing mind?

lg.l: Ἦ οὐ σὲ διδάξουσιν, σοί τ' ἀγγελέουσιν ἐκεῖνοι,
Εἰδότης πραπίδεσσιν ἐναίσιμα μυθολογεῦντες;

p.s: Can a rush grow in the marshes without mud?
Can seaweed and water-nourished reed grow apart from a thirsty land, from a moist one?
While it is green and flourishing, before the harvest it withers faster than grass, and in an unseemly season it dries up.
"Such is the lot of mortals, and such are the ways of all who by transgressions have forgotten God."
For his hope, reckless and airy, shall perish.
His hope is indeed empty, and his confidence shall be feeble, like wretched cobwebs bringing death to flies.
And these things were poured out fine above the rafters, which one might see, by the treacherous weavings of a spider.
"Suddenly an evil storm of wind swept them away.
And his house will always be weak and ready to fall;
Leaning on it he will overthrow it, and his house will not yet stand securely, nor will it be propped well with his hands.
Like a thriving olive shoot that a man tends in a lonely place, which blossoms with white flower, beautiful, luxuriant, a plant as in the joy of a garden;
And coming suddenly, a wind with a great tempest, it twisted him out of his pit, and he was stretched out upon the ground;
"So then he straightway perished.
Or as a tall oak, "whose roots, thick and continually joined together in many stones, are fixed upon a hill;
But not even so did he escape the din of wood-cutting men;
And they came holding wood-cutting axes in their hands, and hurrying they cut him with bronze;
But she, having fallen, groaned, and her lofty tresses were mingled with dust.
"As he blooms for a little time, not at all for long, rejoicing in fleeting splendor and glory;
Suddenly he perishes, and his own place disowns him. "So he spoke." I have never seen you with my eyes.
This is his end, and a joy of evil paths: 'Other men will soon sprout from the dust, rising up later, far better than he.'
For the Immortal will never thrust away a righteous man, nor will he be a helper to evil men, but those who yield to violence devise reckless things.
Until he fills his throat with sweet laughter, his breast with gladness, and his lips with your shout of triumph;
Those who clothe themselves in shame will be forever your enemies;
And the tent of the wicked will utterly perish.
Then deeply-grieving, resourceful Job spoke to him: 'I know;'
Why do you tell all this to me, who know it well?
I know, I understand;
these things indeed you declare to one who understands.
For how could any mortal appear righteous before God?

And was there one who, taking courage, would dare to contend against him in dispute, and in judgment do battle with him in a dread contest, even if there are a thousand of them? He will not refute a single charge, but will yield to God, though he be a good speaker.
He who is beyond the mind of men, and beyond even strength — both alike — is a wise lord and a mighty warrior.
And who ever hardened his stubborn-necked spirit against him, and was not utterly destroyed by the proud counsels of his mind?
He who shakes the mountains and in his fury overturns them, and mortals do not know how he spoke;
and he nodded to the ground the lofty heads of the mountains enraged.
And in his anger he shook the race of men; beneath, he shook the boundless earth, and all the foundations of trembling Hpeiros were thrown into confusion, and the shaken land was heavy-laden.
He gave command to the sun, and the sun did not rise;
And he held back the light, and checked the shining stars;
He covered the sky, and all the streets were darkened by the dawn and the cloud, and a mist was poured down over Olympus.
Who alone stretched out the starry heaven, and swiftly trod upon the swelling wave of the sea;
He made Arcturus untiring, and the strength of Orion, and the Seven-Paths, which they call the Pleiades, the stars, and the rain-bearing chambers of the moist-blowing South Wind.
Who shows forth thrice-marvellous works, extraordinary signs; who performs very many unattainable, unthinkable wonders.
Going near, God escaped me.
But him I could not see with my eyes either going here or there.
He snatches away easily.
Who could restrain him?
Would you speak in reproach, 'Come now, what sort of thing is this that you have done?'

If God does not choose to let go his wrath, nor is persuaded to cast off his anger and to choose friendship, dread defenders and boasters, men, have stood beneath him, fallen on their knees, and trembling has seized their limbs.
Shall I too, coward that I am, dare to speak against him with words that may be spoken out, and to utter words?
For even if I were a good man and blameless, I would not answer him with hostile words, but I would be a suppliant, and with my voice I would call upon the judge.
If I had called, and God had answered me with a word, yet not even so would he have heeded when he heard my voice.
And as when a dreadful storm of wind rises from on high out of the clouds, or with shrill blasts lashes the whole earth, lashes the whole sea;
How God struck me, pursuing me with a slender whip, having smitten me beyond fate with unseemly blows.
Pierced with ceaseless pains, if he allowed me to breathe a little from misery, yet he subdued me with Peucedanian shafts, and made me wholly bitter.
If indeed I am mindful of strength, yet he has advanced in power.
But if I should speak of ordinances and lovely judgment, who could appoint a day, that I might plead with him in justice?
If indeed I claim to be righteous and blameless, then let my tongue and my speech be witnesses against me.
I say I am perfect?
I shall appear crooked-minded.
But if I were blameless, I would not care for my life;
I would wish now to have died, or to live.
Therefore I said, he destroys alike the unjust and the good;
The lot is equal for the good man, and even if one does great evils;
Alike dies the wicked man and he who has done good deeds.
When suddenly he subdues the tribes of mortals with a scourge, and alike laughs at the grief of an innocent man.
He has given the scepter of the earth to a violent, insolent man, who has covered the eyes of law-administering men, of those who set things straight, so that nothing might be upright in judgment.
But if it is not so, where or who is he who will do these things?
My life is swifter than the lightest runner, who runs very swiftly, trusting in his swift feet;
And it has sped swiftly past, like a feather, or a thought;
My days have flown away, and I have never seen anything good.
They have sped past like ships with linen wings that cross the sea, swifter than a breath, or than an arrow from the bowstring;
Or like an eagle, rushing eagerly through dark clouds, wherever it may find some prey and booty.

If ever I speak, I shall forget my calamity but a little, ceasing from weeping and gathering my spirit into my mind — for no profit comes from chill lamentation — so long do I terribly fear lest countless grievous pains be in my mind.
as many as leaves and flowers come to be in season;
as I was ceaselessly struck with dread around and about my spirit.
And this I know clearly, that you will not let me go innocent.
But if I am a transgressor and still am, why then has my heart toiled in vain, for a work that comes to nothing?
If indeed, having bathed my body in snow-white water, and washed my hands, I cleanse away all filth—

But you will cast me into a pit, and you will make me foul, defiled with mire and clay all over my limbs, from foot to head; and from my skin a bitter festering stench would drip, wasting my dear tunic.
For he is not, like me, a weak mortal, that I might be persuaded.
Nor is there any among men who eat the fruit of the earth, so that I might reply, and plead with him in judgment.
Nor is there any mediator between us both who attends us, who might loose the case and change us too, putting an end to strife and quarrels with kindly words.
Let him cease from blows, and keep his rod away from me, and let him no longer terrify me with dreadful fears.
And then, having taken courage, I would gladly speak whatever I know, I wish to speak out plainly, trusting in prudent thoughts.
But God did not spin me such prosperity, as I am worn down by sorrows.
But now it is necessary to endure nevertheless.
Woe is me, wretched man!
Why then should my end be the longest?
How welcome to me would the end of life be!
Would that I had died!
But my heart has held onto life.

I will speak whatever grief in my breast bids me, for it is no reproach, when one has a bitter spirit in his heart, to weep for his misery and, lamenting, to murmur, and to tell aloud all the sorrows he has suffered, groaning heavily.
But I will speak at least to God: Do not judge me by your own standard; show me why you are so angry with me as I grieve.
Is it then pleasing to you to oppress your own works?
Are the handiworks of your hands then to be rejected?
Or do you pursue a destructive purpose against sinful mortals? Do you wish your sweet light to shine upon their eyes?
For what kind are your eyes, since you are one who sees all?
Are they then fleshly and like those of a mortal man?
Do you have eyes and a head like a wretched mortal?
Do you see as a man does, whose light is dim?
Are your days gone by just like those of mortal men?
Is your life indeed passed by, and have the seasons turned about as months wane and years roll round, just as for a man whom his mother bore but for a little while?
Since you persistently inquire into my guilt, tracking down footprints and searching out every sin.
For well you know this, that I am not lawless.
But no one is able to rescue from your hands.
I myself boast that I am the great handiwork of your hand, which you fashioned most swiftly, me who before was nothing, well and skillfully, both forward and backward.
He fashioned me;
but nevertheless you were about to spare me.

Consider now your work, and cast it into your mind, O offspring — remember me, O Lord, and let not forgetfulness seize you, that long ago you molded me like clay, which the potter too labored over with the many-skilled thoughts of his mind.
And will you bring me back again into dust and mother earth?
As when rennet, hastening, curdles white milk that is liquid, and it is quickly turned about, churning it.
Thus then you poured me out, and like cheese you curdled me.
You clothed me with skin and flesh all around; you covered my body with skin and flesh, you knit me together with close-set bones and joints, and you bound me with fat bones and sinews.
Willingly you granted me life and favor.
Your all-seeing eye preserved my soul, and it nourished it and gave the life-sustaining breath that came first.
And you have these things within you, and you brood over them in your heart;
But I know well, indeed, that these things are prepared by you.
If ever I do wrong, you, stretching a most avenging eye, mark me, and you will not let me go unpunished.
Woe is me, wretched that I am, if ever I was made wicked;
But if I am righteous, and know what is fitting in my heart, even so it is not lawful for me to hold a proud spirit;
I am filled with shame, and you look upon my misery.
For it is exceedingly harsh, and it grows ever with the season.
And as when a ravening lion, mountain-bred, trusting in its strength, which, when it has found a horned stag or a wild goat in the glens, springs forth with evil intent;
So you now pursue me, a cowardly and strengthless man, eagerly;
and presently again you will do dreadful things against me too;
You stir up whips against me, very much witnesses of dread wrath, O Ilados; and thick upon one another, hostile battles, wars, and fights are upon me.
Why did you bring me forth out of the womb, O cruel one?
Would that I had died and met my fate, so that no eye had ever seen me, while I was still unfinished in the womb of my mother!
Would that no one had ever seen me with their eyes.
Such was I, wretched man, as though my mother had never borne me, and I had never seen the light, and as I was when I came into being;
Forthwith, carried from the womb, I came to the grave, where I would now be lying, overcome by soft sleep.
Is not my life but few days, and short-lived?

Leave me alone, so that I may breathe a little before my misery, before I go to the place from which I shall not return, to the murky land, where the dark death-demon dwells, and dread shadow, and gloomy night;

lg.l: Πρίν με μολεῖν, ὅθεν οὐ μέλλω πάλιν ἀπονέεσθαι,
Γαῖαν ἐς ἀχλυόεσσαν, ὅθι κὴρ ἀμφιμέλαινα,
Καὶ σκιὴ ὀλομὴ ναίει, καὶ νὺξ ἐρεβεννή·

p.s: To a dark region, darker than gloom itself — is it so? — does a death mighty-limbed hold shadowy halls?
Is it so? The whole world is chaos, and its light is mist.
Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said to him:
Truly he, greatly angered, rebuked him with a harsh speech:
Should one not refute a babbling, shameless tongue?
Will a man of boundless chatter be very superior in judgments?
Or will a word-slinger win his case, who clamors, and who knows in his mind words both disorderly and many?
Truly, would they be silent in silence at your lies, since you babble windy nonsense?
Truly, for what did you say?
Since it is not at all fitting for you to mock Labragoras;
and will anyone convict you of talking nonsense?
Will no one, I tell you, reproach that speech, as many companions as there are, nor speak back, when you utter mockeries?
Ah, do you reproach me with shamelessness? What a thing you have said!
Pure, to my mind, is my life, and blameless the work of my hands, and I declare that I am faultless in my own sight.
Would that an Immortal had spoken clearly to you face to face, pouring from his throat a truthful voice, and announcing to you the mysteries of divine wisdom!
For it is double.
concerning which we are able to know.
And another thing I will tell you, so attend in your heart.
The honor that you pay to God, as much as he is worthy, you do not fully give, as much as he has great need of from you.
But he demands a penalty for wickedness far less.
Can you, by searching, walk in the divine footsteps of God, and by tracking find out the Immortal clearly?
To find and to know (you think, but you are not deceived) what and how great he is in virtue, in honor, and in strength?
But to trace him out is most difficult, higher than the starry Heaven, and deeper than Hades itself, where beneath the earth is the deepest pit.
What then can you accomplish?
But what could you understand?
It is longer than the boundless earth, which is stretched out most in length beneath bright Olympus;
Nor is its breadth so great as that of the dread, unfathomable Ocean, which is crowned around the boundless earth.
If he cuts off, and restrains wicked men, or if he gathers his servants in a mass into one place with all speed, who will reproach his deed, as much as he has done?
For he surely knows men, all who are worthless, and how he fawns upon them with the follies of his mind;
He has seen the wickedness and the reckless deeds of men, and will he not, though he considers well, understand these things in his own heart?
A worthless man, born like a man, is like a foolish colt of a wild ass, and a simpleton, who has no mind, not even a little, and does not wish to be prudent, nor to be among the minds of others.
If then your heart is ready and your spirit hopeful, and you were hastening with prayers and gentle supplications, with outstretched hands eager to propitiate God—
If you have cast wickedness far from your hands, and iniquity does not dwell in your house—
Then your splendor will shine undefiled to look upon, gleaming greatly with beauty and graces, and with youth.
You will stand securely, no trembling will any longer shake your limbs;
But you will forget your misery, and your pains, all of them, which stir you up;
Your trouble will pass away very easily, like a wave of the much-rolling sea.
Your life thereafter will be brighter than the light of the sun, when it has mounted even the middle of the sky;
Smiling sweetly at something, and the boundless upper air rejoices;
From every side, and a white gleam runs around the sky.
You will shine out brightly, like the fair dawn.
And then you will lie down unharmed, sleeping peacefully.
And upon your breast your mind shall be fearless, because there is still hope;
And you will dig round about a trench, at ease, and you yourself shall be a prey of your possessions;
You shall lie in your bed, and no one shall stir up fear for you;
Many shall entreat you, taking hold of your knees.
But the eyes of men whose concern is wretched deeds shall melt from their head, so that they be no longer escapable;
But hope has perished for them, even that which they were expecting to be unending; and it passes away lightly, as when a man breathes out his spirit, and the breath has flown from his lips.
Then noble Job answered him in reply, ever pondering in his breast a mind that had endured much trial:
O friends, surely you alone are men;
or indeed wisdom is with you, and it attends you while you remain, but it will depart to Hades when you have died.
And I indeed have a mind;
but I am not inferior to you;
But who does not clearly know that such things are so?
I am a noble man subdued by grievous ruin, who once was a laughing-stock and a mockery to his own kinsmen, (and they laughed sweetly at him even as he grieved.
) And he entreated God, and God heard him greatly.
But nevertheless, for a righteous and blameless man, who was indeed such, many mocked him, and he has become a plaything to them.

Whoever rolls about hoping to live, thinking he will fall, already having fallen to his knees and having met with great woe — such a man, cowardly, breathing smoke, cowering in the smoke, worthless and dim, is seen in his mind to be so — compared to a man very well-favored, who has not endured so many sorrows.
But the tents and fair dwellings of robbers flourish continually in great feasting.
Those who provoke God — to them he has stretched out great wealth, and has poured down wondrous riches upon them for a day.
The impious live, paying no heed to God's regard.
Now ask the beasts, and they will teach you;
And question the birds of the air, and the bird will report to you;
Or speak to the earth, and it will remind you;
And the fish of the sea will tell you, as many as the swell of the sea nourishes.
For among all these, who is there that has not known this, that the hand of God alone has wrought all these things?
In whose hand is the life-breath of every living thing, of all that breathe upon and creep on the earth, the spirit and life of men that walk on the ground.
Does not the sound of words stir the hearing ear?
Does not the palate well know the tasting of food and drink, judging what pleases a man in his mind, or what is bitter?
Thus with elders there is much knowledge of mind, and with many days good sense attends together.
Truly long-lived men are much-knowing, and the reverend ones increase in understanding as life grows.
Therefore with the Almighty King are wisdom and strength.
He who is supreme in the counsel of men, and supreme in understanding all things, since an endless age stands for him.
He cast down and destroyed.
Who could build again?
He shut and confined alike.
Who then would open it again?
For the thirsty land, water from the earth he destroyed, and its moisture.
And he sent down rains when the clouds were heavy-laden, and beneath the storm the whole dark earth is weighed down.
And beside him are strength and lovely self-restraint;
And both of these, by the will of the great God, are his: he who casts wicked deceit, and he who is deceived, he who is caught in baneful snares, and he who deceives.
At another time, having stripped and taken captive those who held shrewd counsels in their minds as rulers, he destroyed the understanding of judges;
At another time again he shattered over-mighty kings, and loosed the strong bonds of tyranny, and he shut them up, having bound them in prison, and around their waists he cast a belt upon the hip.
Trusting in his manliness, having stripped and led away people-devouring leaders of peoples and also rulers, whose strength was feeble, and having taken away their goods.
Often he confounded the words of the most trusty companions;
If I spoke any word dear to their hearts among one another—
a good thing—straightway the storm-winds snatch it up and carry it off;
He has put profitless counsel of limbs in the breasts of elder men, and taken away their good wits.
And upon rulers he poured dejection and reproach;
But these straightway become the most despised of the living.
And those who in strength and might were pre-eminently the best before—their great fury has laid them low, and loosed the headband;
And straightway there is no other mortal feebler than these.
And as many things as have been hidden beneath the innermost recesses of the earth, he drew them out from the deep;
and outside the middle mist he brought forth into the light the black shadow of death.
He made many nations grow, and again he destroyed a people;
And these are countless by the will of the great God; those who murmur against God when he has murmured against them are brought low;
He kept confounding tribes, and again he kept diminishing peoples.
He easily terrified the kings upon the earth, and by force he struck them down even though they were mighty;
So for them, grieving, their dear heart was broken, and wandering in a trackless desert they roam astray;
They grope with their hands in the misty darkness, and they do not see the light, wandering about like drunkards, to whom he gave a favorable spirit of mind, and loosed their limbs.
O friends, all these things have not come to pass unknown in my presence.
But I know, and I have learned, and I have seen with my eyes; I was indeed inquiring from them, and I heard with my ears a report.
But I know as much as you do.
Since I am not inferior to you in understanding or in nature, though you think very deeply.
Would that I could speak to God!
My spirit bids me bring a quarrel before the immortal King of justice, and to display my arguments, and to enter a mighty contest.
But you are liars and reckless deceivers, adorned with fabricated falsehoods in your portions.
A physician is a man worth many others, but you are worthless physicians, feeble and cruel, and you do not yet know how to heal my grief.
Do not now, I pray, sit beside me and mutter one thing, each from a different side.
Would that you would be wholly silent, and cease from your words!
And then would you be like men of understanding.
Hear me, companions, who speak wicked things, and understand the disputatious words of our lips.
Will you be boasters, showing favor to God?
Or is it dear to you to speak windy nonsense on his behalf?
Will you ever be advocates for God in judgment?
Or will you bring favor to him in judgment?
And having contended for him against adversaries, since now strife has arisen, will you be his helpers?
Is this one in need of you?
How I wish that your mind (may this be better) and your counsels were drawn out, and that I might test you!
Will you mock him as a man mocks men?
If indeed by transgression you set crooked laws, and afflict others and secretly show favor to others, this one in turn will greatly rebuke you and will convict you.
Will not his surpassing glory terribly confound you?
And will a dread, a wondrous thing, and fear terrify you exceedingly?
And your memories become like ashes, and your bodies like bodies of clay.
Be silent, and I too will be still, and let me alone a little while, that I may tell you all the truth.
Let the Immortal punish me as much as is fitting, let him do as he wishes, and as is dear to his heart.
Why then do I take up my foul flesh with my teeth, the wretched wounds of my body, clutching at the dust that is my mother?
Why then, exposing my life to danger, do I cast it away relentlessly, while it ever stands on the razor's edge?
Even if he shuts me in, I shall nevertheless trust in him, and I shall take courage in him, and in the midst of destruction;
But even so I shall prove my righteousness before him.
He who is my mighty light and helper shall be so;
For no deceiver shall come before him.
Lend me your ears, and hear my voice;
So that I may say what my spirit within my breast urges.
For now I have set my case in order, and my proofs have been armed all together; truly I have marshalled dense phalanxes of arguments for fierce war, and they are eager to fight with might.
I know that I shall win, and I shall soon appear blameless.
Who now will tell me, and will plead with me in justice?
But if I sit thus silent, grieved in heart, straightway I shall breathe my last, and the bonds of silence will strangle me.
But have mercy, Lord, and set a gracious heart within you, and now keep these two evils away from me; then I shall dare to come before you.
First, then, keep your heavy hands away from me, and then do not trouble me with your dread terrors.
Meanwhile you call on me, and I will answer back again;
Or I too will speak plainly, and you answer with a word.
How many are my transgressions, how many my sins?
Show me my transgression and my sin, so that I may know.
Why then have you hidden your face from me?
And why, being angry as at an enemy, have you grown wrathful?
Will you break off a leaf that is shaken hither and thither?
Or will you pursue it with a dry stalk, with a whip?
For against me you have written many very bitter and grievous evils, as in a book, things that ought not to have come into the light.
And you have wreathed around me the faults of my erring youth;
All that I did long ago in grievous childishness, these things you have now reminded me of, and the things that I now, wretched, enjoy.
And around my feet, so that they may never be able to escape, you placed stocks and fetters, and shameful bonds.
You stretch a most exact eye upon all my footprints, and you have set a seal around both my feet.

And thus someone might say, looking at another nearby: "Do you not see how this man, in his follies, has utterly perished miserably, and how he has melted away like something rotten, and like a garment, which becomes the spoil and prey of a moth?"

As far as a mortal exists and has sucked the breast of a woman, his days upon the earth are few, and his life becomes short-lived, and the end of death quickly overtakes a man, and from his scant strength he lives as a wretched one among others.
For there is not yet anything more wretched than a man, of all creatures that breathe upon the earth and creep.

He comes forth like a flower, and is cut down; he flees also as a shadow, and continues not. A mother reared him as a plant in the garden of an orchard, but at once he is short-lived and wretched beyond all; he became so, to whom an evil fate bore and reared a mother.
For he is cut off and withers away utterly, and is dried up.
He is gone, flown away like a shadow, or even like a dream; he abides among the living but a little while, not at all for long.
Do you indeed look upon such things with your eyes, marking sharply all transgressions and faults?
And do you come to meet me when I am judged in court?
Who could bring a clean thing out of an unclean?
(Never anyone.
) Or who has come forth pure from the womb of a woman?
His days are appointed; the number of his months is with you, and you have set a limit which he cannot pass.
And the limits which you set, which he would not overstep even a little.
Leave him alone for that, so that he may rest a little from his misery, until he finishes the life-course he has run, like a hireling who, having completed his toil, may receive a shameful wage.
There is hope for a tree, if with the long-edged bronze, being cut, it lets tender leaves fall to the ground;
It will sprout again, and again it will grow leaves and branches, once it has first left the cutting in the mountains.
Even if a root grows old in a thirsty land, and a dry stem dies under much drought;
But even afterward, by some life-loving nature, it will sprout, whenever abundant water-channels are present;
And by these it rejoices as a newly-nourished plant, as before, and it bursts forth again with flowers, since it drank moisture in abundance.
For even if it withers for a time, yet this again revives it: the life-giving scent of waters breathes upon it.
But a man, a feeble man, swiftly fated, passes away; the cowardly mortal breathes out his spirit — and where is he?
As water fails from the grey sea, and upward the vapour is drawn by the sun's force, and the deep diminishes;
As the stream of a river that is dried up has perished;

As a mortal sleeping in the dust will never rise again from beneath the murky darkness, nor will he sicken before he no longer looks up at the starry heaven above the earth, but always he will lie securely, subdued by mighty sleep.
Would that you had hidden me in a grave beneath the earth, and kept me hidden in the inner chamber, until your wrath should be sent down.
Would that you would appoint me a time, and remember me.
If a man has died, shall he live again among the living?
For this reason I too wait unceasingly for all the fated days of my life, awaiting until, having fulfilled the portion of life, the end of death overtakes me.
Then you will call me, and I shall answer you again;
Longed-for.
For you, truly, the works of your hands, the cunning crafts of your hands, will be pleasing to your heart.
You weigh all my footsteps very carefully, having perceived keenly, and you watch for my goings, whether here or there as I go.
But he is the watcher and overseer of my transgressions.
Truly my transgression is sealed up as in a pouch, and you have stitched together all my evil devices.

He brought down the shadowy mountains into the dust; the peaks and the topmost headlands of the lofty mountains were consumed with their very roots; and beneath, the earth was thrown into confusion, and the foundations of the towering rocks were shaken.
Water wears away stone, and the flood sweeps the rock away, and a boundless rainstorm has washed away the things that grow from the ground.
But you destroyed the whole hope of wretched mortals.
You thrust a wretched man down continually, and he is gone.
At your moving, his countenance is turned now here, now there.
But you cast him off harshly, though he has dense griefs in his mind.
His sons come to honor, but he does not see them;
And soon again they dwindle, though they were very illustrious;
But he does not know any longer of glory, nor of any mourning.
But dread grief will cover his mind all-dark, pierced through his limbs with sharp pains;
With weeping and groaning, his dear heart grieved, he will have woeful sorrows, and inwardly he will lacerate his spirit.
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said to him, and mocking him rebuked him with a harsh word:
Will a babbling man truly be wise, one who in his own heart foolishly knows disorderly and empty things?
And like a well-made wineskin that is stuffed full?
Will he fill his belly with wind, so that he may babble windy nothings, such as the storm-winds carry off snatching up many things?
In which will he be judged with unprofitable words?
Is it with idle words, which do not profit men?
Wicked man, who in your heart reveres God, and still respects him, and does not at all regard his own soul, nor are you willing to be softened, nor are you touched by gentle prayers.
But you have grown bold still further, and you have spoken an overbearing word.
For your mouth has openly recounted your wickedness, and your tongue, which is adorned with your guiles, the things you utter, like a crafty and thievish deceiver.
Thus, you see, it is dear to you to speak deceitful things.
Not I, but your own mouth judges against you; your lips again testify against you that you are babbling.
Are you really the firstborn of mortals?
The most ancient of men?
Or were you born long ago, before the great mountains were made?
Have divine mysteries really been revealed to you from heaven?
Therefore have you appeared alone wise among mortals?
What do you know, that they are but shadows that flit?
But why—what is it that you know, that we ourselves do not know clearly?
We?
Or what do you know, that would be unclear to us?
since we are not at all lacking in understanding.
And indeed there are among us men born long ago, full of knowledge, and very reverend grey-templed elders, who are older than your father.
Is it indeed that the consolations of God are worthless, and whatever he may give, trusting in kindnesses, is a word?
For surely he knew how to be gentle to all.
Is it indeed that some oracles were whispered in your own heart, as you ponder hidden things, which are unknown even to others?
Why does your heart swell within you as you ponder, O wretch?
Or what has put you into such speechlessness?
Why do you wink in this way, and nod with your brows?
Why then have your eyes thus closed beneath your eyelids?
Why, thinking great things against the Immortal in your heart, do you rage madly, and fierce madness has entered you?
Wretch, what word has escaped the fence of your teeth?
What is man, that he should be pure?
Or what is woman-born, that he should be righteous?
For not even his blameless servants are trustworthy, and those who are most loyal and dearest to him of all;
Nor yet is the heaven, starry with its most gracious radiance, pure in his eyes to behold.
How much more so a man who is hateful and shameful?
A man insatiable of lawlessness, before whom would you appear?
Who even with thirsty spirit gulped down sin, as when one gulping greedily drinks bright water, parched with thirst, and his spirit urges him to drink;
So he in his wickednesses drank insatiably with thirsty frenzy.
For I will speak something from my own knowledge; but do you attend and hear me, O Angelos; this I have long seen with my own eyes.
And did the wise from of old learn it from their own fathers?
To us they recounted it continually, and they told it forth.
To them alone God gave the whole land, and stretched out the tribes.
And no foreigner at all dwelt any longer among them.
The wicked man writhes in pains all his days, with tears and groaning, and with griefs, racking his soul.
For him, both outrage and violence reach the iron heaven; he has not seen many revolving years.
He perished in his youth, and he came to the threshold of old age.
A dreadful sound rang about his ears; and the destroyer, having caught him unawares as he flowed on well, seized him suddenly, and slew him though he did not perceive it.
He does not indeed think that he will return out of the darkness, and the sword awaits him, very thirsty, raging with blood.

He is worn down by wandering, and like a wretched, weary, famished vagrant longing somewhere for food he roams over the people and city of men of alien speech; he hopes that grim doom and the pitiless day stand near him, when darkness covers him about with terror and great fear of grief arises, and he is seized by strength, as a chieftain trusting in his might, armed in blazing bronze for the fierce war.

lg.l: Ταρβοσύνῃ καὶ πένθος ἔοι μέγα δεῖος ἐνόρσει,
Κὰδ δ' ἕλεν ἰσχύσει, ὡς ὄρχαμος ἀλκὶ πεποιθὼς
Ἄχριον ἐς πόλεμον κεκορυθμένος αἴθοπι χαλκῷ.

p.s: He stretched out his hand against the Immortal in overweening fashion, and he hardened his own great-hearted spirit against himself.
But rushing upon him, and raging with shameless onset, he charged straight at his neck, and at the bossed shield well fitted all through with close-set nails.
He covered his face with fat and flesh, rich and sleek, and much belly bulged out over his sturdy thigh and his long knee.
He dwells in cities made desolate, and in houses that no one values, which are already about to become heaps.
He shall not have many possessions, and his wealth shall be short-lived, nor shall it be at all steadfast upon the much-nourishing earth.
Nor shall he ever pass out of the misty darkness, nor ever out of ruin and wretched misery.
As god-sent fire rages through the deep glens of a parched mountain, and the deep forest burns, and the wind, shaking it everywhere, wraps the flame about.
As fire sent from God devours his branches, so the breath of God's mouth scorches the flame.
Truly his mind, wandering and trusting in wretched folly, vainly grasped at great gifts;
Therefore his reward shall be empty and worthless.
His prosperity, not yet green, shall perish swiftly-fated from the root, withered, all-unseasonable, quickly faded.
He shall strip off the unripe grape as he gathers it, and even the one still growing fleshy, like a vine thrice-blighted, unripe, harsh.
But swiftly it will shed its blossoms, like the fruit-destroying olive tree.
As a tent would be desolate of a reckless deceiver, and he would become childless, and God would strip him bare.
But those who love possessions, for whom gifts are pleasing, their fair houses would smolder with fire from top to bottom.
They who conceive toil and grievous transgression, give birth to wickedness, and hold deceits in their belly.
Then much-enduring noble Job answered him, groaning exceedingly, and he lamented more in his heart:
Truly I have heard many such things before.
O companions, evil companions, having a harsh spirit, you are cruel friends, jealous beyond others, wretched and worthless comforters of my calamity.
O Eliphaz, you have quite touched me in spirit with your rebuke;
But you will never cease babbling vain things. Why do you afflict me, who have griefs in my strong heart?
Why does your heart and proud spirit urge you on?
Do you rush in so recklessly?
since there is no need of it at all.
Was it in reliance on someone that you answered me with such a hateful word?
And I too could speak as you do, if your soul were in my soul's place — if equal fate had subdued you, and if you had suffered as many evils as I have suffered and toiled with unceasing heart.
And I too could strengthen you with my mouth, if I wished, and shake my head at you and utter reproaches.

But rather may I strengthen my worn-out companions with some soothing word, and may there be a sweet-honeyed remedy for your groans and griefs, whatever I may say to you who are distressed, loosening lips that end pain.
But why now do I speak these things among you in vain?
For I cannot forget the mind of joyless misery, nor do I think I ever will, either in words or in silence.
But I groan continually, and digest countless sorrows by day and by night, and there is no respite from my trouble.
Because the heavenly King has crushed me, a wretched man, with grievous toil, and has bound me in heavy ruin;
And he has made me a solitary wanderer, and has scattered my dear companions.
With hollow wrinkles he has furrowed my countenance, and he has withered my fair skin upon my bent limbs, and ugly wrinkles bear witness against me;
And my body has become thin and wasp-like.

He who greatly confounds me, and has torn me apart with a pitiless heart, having torn away my skin, since he rages relentlessly — my enemy has gnashed his destructive teeth at me, and glaring at me he stretched his eye like a flame.
But those hostile men gaped at me, the wretches, and they struck me with unseemly blows, and they smote my cheek with their violent hands, and they rose up against me and gathered together.
God, being angry with me, has handed me over to the hands of the wicked, to become a prey and a spoil for impious men.
Though I was at ease, he shattered my dear heart; and seizing me by the head and by the neck at the joint, he broke me limb from limb, and set me up as his target.
And his archers encircled me with terrible shafts, and having marshalled themselves in close array like a tower.
He shattered my kidneys with his unsparing right hand, and cut me in three and in four pieces, and did not spare.
He smote all my inward parts, and poured out my gall to the ground.
He smote my skin with blow upon blow; like a monstrous giant he leapt upon me, one against whom my spirit within my breast most of all rages in its strength.
I sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and covered myself with torn, filthy rags, defiled with foul smoke.
And my honor was defiled in the dust, and my glory has perished.
Grievous tears have furrowed my dear cheeks, and they have made my eyes, once very beautiful, grow dim;
And the shadow of death sat upon my eyelids.
Nor do I suffer pains because of my own ruin;
For I am not reckless, nor one who knows wickedness in his heart;
For I do not reproach myself for a prayer, nor for a hecatomb, which I once offered to him;
and my prayer is blameless.
Do not hide my blood beneath your depths, O earth, nor ever by my cry give me a recess where it may lie hidden.
Even now, high in the clouds, my witness dwells in my house, and my witness is in the starry heaven.
My companions mock me, and I am a plaything to my friends; but before God I pour out pitiful tears from beneath my brows, countless tears from my eyes, these flow for me, grieving at heart.
O that it were lawful for a man to plead with God as a man does with his fellow, and to come to trial in court, as when a friend contends in judgment against a friend.

But I, when a few years had rolled round, after I had lived but a little while among the living — and no longer for long — straightway going (for life is spent quickly, and fate is near, and he has set forth days, and my lifetime has passed by in wandering portions, and a little share is still left to me, wretched man, for my mother bore me to sail downward) — I shall sink into Hades, and shine among the dead, hastening my step into the unturning land, whence I shall come no more.
But God took away my return home.
And I lie here with little strength, and a little breath still remains in me; already, as I grow feeble, they have quenched the life-giving breath in me.
My days have been quenched, and my life is short.
Now I am struck by lightning, and graves are ready for me.
Are not mockers and slanderers here beside me?
Do I not see them face to face, when they speak mockeries?
And I do not know their insults, and I see them with my eyes unceasingly, which stir me in my heart?
Shall I not through the night take delight, thinking on the evils I have endured, I to whom eyes and heart are hateful, and for whom sweet sleep has perished?
But I beseech you, Lord, and do you give heed and listen to me. Come now, stand surety, give a pledge to be guaranteed, one who would speak most rightly of justice for us both.
And who will cut faithful oaths for me, and take my hand?
For you put a foolish heart in their breasts, and I utterly blamed their minds, who said:
Therefore you will not at all grant them any greater glory.

Whoever has ensnared a friend with guile, babbling deceitful things, announcing good things but brooding evil in his heart, at last for his dear children his eyes will melt from the middle of his head, so that some one even of late-born men may learn by his eyes a shameful blindness.
He made me a reproach and a byword to others, and among them I was a laughingstock, like the sound of a drum; I became a toy and a joy to infant children.
But let my eyes waste away from unceasing laments, and with much weeping, and with a pouring of tears.
And all my limbs go like a dim shadow.
And at this a grave would await the pious, as they perceived.
Whoever he himself is blameless, and already blameless, so that a storm may rush upon him with reckless deceit.
But the righteous man holds firmly to his own path, not swerving aside, whenever by purity of hands he keeps great strength ever for upright men.
But come, hither, friends (the minds of good men are changeable); now, turned back, you might recover from sickness.
For among you there is not even one man to choose who thinks wisely.
