Ah me, since my life shall be darkened, being unstable;
My days have gone by as the months roll round; my life has run its course, like a chariot's wheel rolled along.
My plans are scattered abroad, the cares of my heart.
But he changes nights into tearful days; the sun is quenched, and soon again dark evening came.
Truly, then, they count even this a bearable evil, when one weeps for days on end, deeply grieved at heart, and sleep possesses his nights;
(For he forgets all good things and evils, once sleep covers his eyelids.) But even so, through the night, respite from evil comes to me.

While I wait for the day, holding incurable griefs in my heart, a tomb would have been made for me, a shadowy house beneath the earth, where I might sleep and slumber in a brazen sleep, spreading out my bed and shining blankets, wrapped in mist and darkness as in a cloak.
I say to corruption: You are my father.
But to the worm, Mother — you are a mother to me, and a lovely sister.
Of this lineage and blood, I declare, I am.
But now, whence is my hope, or whence has courage come to me?
Who will see these many good things with his eyes?
Things I might hope for, that they may come to me hereafter?
All things will follow me down, and the sinking into the pit.
We shall lie in the dust alike, beneath the bosom of the earth.
Then Bildad the Shuhite, greatly angered, answered him:
How long will you speak such things among us in vain?
Will you not cease from words, so that you may hear our speech?
And I will say something else; but do you lay it in your mind.
Why do you liken us to brute beasts, so great in your eyes?
Why too do you count us as worthless, like the unclean and most reprobate of the living?
You have been exceedingly angry, and you tear your heart within;

But it is possible that at some time the land will be desolate on your account — yes, greatly so — even while he rages in his heart; and no longer shall a rock be moved on your account, trembling in its own foundations, but leaping high it shall set itself on Olympus in the upper air.
There shall be a day when the light of the wicked man perishes, and his lamp is quenched, even of that man as he is destroyed.
No spark from his hearth shall remain, which shall be a flame saving a seed of fire, since the flame has utterly been quenched.

But his house shall be utterly darkened, and there shall be no light for him in his tent from the torches shining beneath Hades, since his own lamp shall be quenched, and he himself shall be quenched.
And his feet are subdued by wandering, and his limbs below, and by his strong might he has turned all his footsteps aside from the broad-wayed road onto a narrow path.
Truly, by his wicked plots he shall straightway perish nameless.
Into a groaning snare, having wandered under his own feet, he fell through his follies, and in a noose he set his foot.
A treacherous snare seized him by the heel, and around his feet it was woven, poured all about, and an evil bond subdued him.
But his guilty, violent-handed robber snatches away all his livelihood, and cuts down his branches.
Truly, whenever he is about to set his feet, on every side along the paths, from the ground thick snares spring up here and there, lurking, unchangeable in form, so that they may never be escapable.
Fear and trembling will distress his spirit all around, and dreadful bogey-shapes with grim faces, glaring terribly, will frighten him.
Thus then fear seized that man, and panic, the companion of chilling fear.
But his strength and might shall be consumed by grievous famine, and destruction stands ready, very near to him.
The firstborn of death shall devour his strength, gnawing his sinews in the firm joint of the flesh.
And all hope of his house and tents is perished, and his confidence.
And a hateful fate led him to the king of terrors, and to the steward of fears.
Because from another's livelihood he built his own house, therefore a dread trembling lingered upon his tents;
Truly it was shaken all over, struck by God's thunderbolt, and a dread flame of burning brimstone arose.
His root shall be withered and devoid of moisture; below the root shall be dry, and above it a misshapen trunk, the branch of one cut off, and the fruit of one withering.
His memory shall perish from the earth, and his good fame as well;
He shall be unknown to all, unheard-of, nameless, for all days among men who may come hereafter.
And they shall cast him far from the light of the sun into darkness, driving him from the land with a rebuke, saying: Begone, evil eyeball, evil beast, begone!
Begone from the world more swiftly, you reproaches of the living!
Nor indeed do children prattle at his knees; he will have no son, nor offspring in his people, nor then any survivor dwelling in his house.
It will be alike a great wonder even for those to come to hear of, how the grave held those who were before, as they were seen.
A day of necessity and misery, which came upon him.
Such was the house of sinful men, and such their lot, whose deeds were cruel, who pay no heed to God and do not revere him in their heart.
Then again noble Job, deeply groaning, answered him:
He wailed piteously, and spoke a lamenting word:
Woe is me, that I spoke thus; so much have I suffered at the hands of my companions.
How long will you batter my spirit with harsh reproach?
How long will you crush me with mocking words?
Now indeed ten times you insult me with grievous outrage, and there is no shame, since your mind is disobedient.
But you regard me as some foreigner and a stranger.
Often in my follies I was willingly sinning, I erred, I went astray, trusting in my painful mind.
For I do not refuse.
(what mortal would not sin?
) But what is that to them and to you?
let all these things be my concern;
My ruin is with me; let no other care about it.
But if it is dear to you, quarreling with a comrade, to utter reproaches idly and not in due order, and to pour abuse on me because of my grievous misery, and to heap up reproof, when I have toiled—
Know that the Almighty has bound me with heavy ruin, and with his hand has dragged me, and I fell straightway headlong;
He has cast his net around me, and I am entangled all about, like a fish in a many-eyed net;
If ever I cried out from outrage, a word undiluted,
being worn down;
and I have cried aloud, yet no one grants me justice.
Having blocked my paths from every side, he made them impassable for me;
with mist and clouds he covered over my way.
I was held mighty and revered among men formerly in feasts, and much grace shone forth;
But now again my glory has perished, and God has taken away all my splendor, and has stripped the garlands from my head.
He has dashed me on every side, and I am gone, and like a tree cut down with bronze that brings its tender leaves to the ground, hurling them down with its very roots continually—
Thus I too fall, and all hope for me has perished.
He has been exceedingly angry with me, and he holds me as an enemy in his fate.
Against me in a tower-formation his troops gathered together, and they encircled me, and they dug a trench by my tent, like bristling battle-lines of shield-bearers facing the foe.
My own brothers stand aloof from me; those who were once my guests are now mine, and my attendants, who were formerly appointed to me.
Those who were dearest and most beloved to me of all, my kinsmen and likewise my companions, have departed far from me.
Very far off, as if they had utterly forgotten me.
My maidservants and my handmaidens regard me as a stranger, and I seem in their eyes like a foreigner.
I called my servant, but he did not answer me with a word.
I kept supplicating him with gentle words, but he did not listen to my entreaties.

Nor has my wife kept alive at my voice when I spoke, but she has hated me; her breath is loathsome to me, which flows from my mouth terribly as I speak; and it is thankless to his own people, whatever I may say. If I plead even for my dear children and sweet marriage-beds — but I think that she will not be persuaded by me.
Even foolish children despised me, reckless as they were.
For when I rose up, they mocked me with reproachful words.

All who were formerly my own dear companions — never did we speak apart in the assembly, nor in the council, but holding one spirit we were always of one mind — these, when they saw me utterly ruined and perceived my misery, now loathing me have cast off friendship.
Woe is me, that my bones have cleaved to my skin, fleshless, around my limbs, and my members have become shriveled.
I am wasted away with wounds, and my limb has been taken from the edge of my body, unless it was taken from under the roots of the teeth.
O friends, you are friends, have pity on me, inasmuch as I have toiled; pity me, wretched man, and put compassion in your heart, because God has struck me and set me down with a heavy hand.
Why do you pursue me thus, as God does, though I am already worn down?
Is it not enough that my body swells with dripping wounds?
Why then do you still have need of me, when my flesh is perishing?
If you had long devoured it, soon would satiety attend you.
O that my words were written in a many-knowing book, to be learned by generations and by those to come!
O that they were stamped with indelible graven marks!
O that they were engraved with an iron chisel, or with lead, on marble, or on stone!
For I know that he lives, to whom I owe the reward of life, who indeed released me and gave boundless ransom;
That he lives I know clearly, and that hereafter he shall yet stand upon the dry land, when the very last day of the world arrives.
If then this body becomes prey for worms, and maggots and creeping things consume my flesh, yet nevertheless with my flesh I shall see God, having risen again;
I myself, not another on my behalf, with these eyes shall see, and not with others', nor with alien eyes;
Even if my inward parts have rotted, and all my kidneys have perished beneath.
You therefore ought to speak thus: Why now do we torment him?
Why then do we thus vex the soul of our companion with harsh reproaches?
For in my case the ordinances stand fast, in righteousness, like the roots of a thick oak, firmly fitted.
Fear now the sharp sword, for the sword is exacted upon sinful men, so that you may know that judgment and retribution come to be.
And Sophar the Naamathite answered and said to him:
Therefore the cares of my heart urged me on, and therefore I too hasten, eager to speak face to face.
I heard the reproach of me, and the evil outrage, and the rebuke, and my spirit within my breast urges me to utter a word.
Do I indeed know this of old? And do you lay it up in your heart?
Since the time when men first dwelt upon the earth:
Because the wicked exult for but a very short time, and the joy of a proud man lasts only a moment?
Even if his height reaches to the wide heaven, and even if he be mingled among the clouds, exulting greatly in splendor and glorying in renown;
Yet nevertheless he has utterly perished, like all-filthy dung, hateful, whose stench is most deadly.
And now someone then, seeing another nearby, might say: 'Where is that man now, since I no longer see him anywhere?'
But always, at least formerly, he used to appear among the foremost.
He has gone, flown away, like a shadowy dream;
like a phantom, which quickly perished, when sleep released his eyelids;
And now someone seeking him, if he should find him, he has gone off like nocturnal phantoms.
Nor shall an eye see him again, which before had beheld him, nor shall any place, which formerly held him, see him any more.
His sons, who long to appease even the rabble, will charm the mind of the poor with soothing words, and with gentle speech they will fasten upon the needy.
But whatever possessions he took from them by force with a ruthless heart, wishing to please them, he will carry back with his own hands.
But his bones are filled with the sin of his youth, which he committed.
Formerly, while I was still in my youth, when my strength was steadfast; but now, behold, I am seized with hateful wasting throughout my limbs.
It was because of lewdness, and a grievous island attends him, and this one shall be his bedfellow in the dust.
Even if it was sweeter than honey upon his mouth, yet truly under his tongue wickedness was hidden.
Even if he shall swallow it down greedily, yet he did not let it go, but he holds it firmly, and it rushed upon the middle of his throat.
But his food within his bowels was changed, like the gall of a sharp-biting asp was wrought within him.
However greedily he swallowed down wealth and riches, he shall vomit them up again, as when a man, heavy with wine and hungover, retched to the ground, and wine gushed from his throat.
Thus he would vomit up willingly, though with unwilling heart, the goods that he devoured.
But God shall draw them out of his belly.
And then he shall suck the deadly venom of the asp, and the people-destroying viper shall slay him with its own tongue.
May he not see the rivers, nor the fair-flowing streams, nor the rivers of honey, nor the streams of butter.
Never shall he eat the fruit of his toil, but he shall give it back, not yet having tasted it, as one who is of the labor of his hands;
Whatever goods he took from others, so many shall he let go, no longer exulting in his wealth and his many possessions.
Because he used to wear down the poor man with a ruthless heart, and he wickedly sent away the needy man empty-handed;
He seized a house from another, which he himself never built, trusting in his manhood and the strength of his hands;
His belly will be without a share of rest, never filled, pierced with sharp pains;
But desire for these seizes him, will he still save it for tomorrow?
And there will not be even a little left over of his food;
In vain would a man be waiting for his own prosperity, which he will leave behind when he dies;
For truly all things had perished for him.
When he says he has enough, while he thinks he will be satisfied, suddenly a need comes upon him no longer bearable, and in the midst of his feasting a mighty necessity falls upon him;
And he will bring upon him heavy hands of wicked men.

So that he may gladly be about to taste food, just as he stretches out his hands toward the ready viands set before him, upon which God will swiftly cast a heavy-wrathful spirit, and in the midst of the feast (for satiety had not yet come upon him) — as when he pours down thick snowflakes to the ground.
Even if in war he escaped the bronze spear, yet not even so is he about to be safe.

For as you said, a dreadful twang arose from the iron bow; the bow twanged, and the string gave a great cry, and the arrow leapt, sharp-pointed, bringing death and black doom; it pierced him through the middle, and took away his dear life.

It is drawn from the sheath, eager to satisfy itself on flesh, and straight through the tender flesh came the point, and the sharp flashing sword pierced his gall, and all was warmed with his own blood, and it loosed his limbs.
Always a dread terror holds him, and a fear not to be escaped.
All darkness within his house shall be, and a murky gloom in the recesses of his house;
But a divinely-kindled flame, which was roused from its blast, shall utterly ravage him, and if any one was left to him behind in his tent, it shall go ill for him.
Heaven shall make his wickedness manifest, because he has done it;
A fool!
for he said he would escape God's notice;
But the earth will stand in judgment to bring a verdict against him.
But all his wealth has perished, since God was angered, and his goods flowed out of his house like deceitful water.
This is the portion of a man who does not shrink from doing lawless deeds, and this is the decree long since fated for him, a wretched destiny;
for thus the god spun it for him.
Answering him, much-devising Job spoke, ever pondering in his breast a grief-worn mind:
Hear me, my friends, though I suffer evils, and let this too be a comfort to you, whatever I may say.
First allow me to speak a little in turn (for so is right), and afterward you may mock.
Is it against men that I complain?
And if it is even so, how would my dear heart be stirred within my breast?
But listen to me;
swiftly may amazement seize you too, may amazement seize you;
laying a hand upon the mouth.
When therefore I perceived these things, amazement took me, and struck within my spirit I tremble, and trembling seized my limbs.
Why do the wicked live thus in great feasting?
Why too do mortals grow old in misery?
Why too do those who devise reckless things prosper, adorned with bliss and wealth among mortals?
Their children are vigorous, and their offspring are present before them, and they see their children flourishing on both sides, and their children's children.
They dwell in well-built houses in peace, far from all fear, apart from all grief, never being struck by the clear-sounding whip of God.
Their bull is noble, and it does not fail in mounting.
And their cows give birth, and never do they miscarry.

They send them out a little, and in troops like a flock; and the boys sing with dancing and choral piping, and maidens and young men, thinking tender thoughts, danced, holding each other's hands by the wrist.
And among them a boy played the lyre sweetly with a clear-toned phorminx, and sang to the lovely linen string.
And they, whenever they heard the honey-sweet voice of the lyre, were gladdened, and in all their hearts the spirit was warmed; and with song and nimble feet they followed skipping.

Thus they, well clad in cloaks and tunics, ever sleek as to their heads and fair of face, drinking and eating (for they had abundance), rich in livelihood, after they had fulfilled their doom, suddenly went into the house of Hades, into the house of death.
But they hemmed God in with the tonguelessness of their mind, and they cast out a very overweening word:
For as they said, 'Go, depart far away from us as quickly as possible, for we have no wish to know your ways.'
And who is the Almighty, that we should serve him?
Or what profit is it that we have entreated him much, since he has refused, and no relief comes from evil?
But the overbearing will not long be able to boast, for their prosperity is not steadfast, nor is it fixed.
Therefore I too spat out the deceitful counsel of the wicked, nor did their crooked plan win me over, who, yielding to violence, devise reckless things.
How often has hateful darkness seized the impious?
How often has a bitter blast quenched their lamp, coming suddenly, and has grim destruction with all its force subdued the torches as they were being extinguished?
But God, being angry with men, gives them pains, to each one as he wills.
For he is the steward of sorrows.

And they become like dry stubble, which the whirling storm-winds soon snatch away, or like chaff, which the shrill-blowing winds, whipping with the hurricane, drive round in swift-rolling fashion across the threshing floors.
For at another time God here as steward would store up for the children the grievous transgression of the father, and they themselves, paying the price, would enjoy it from their parent.
At another time he himself, the wretched man, used to pay the recompense of his own ruin, and there is no postponement of wickedness.
With his own eyes the all-doomed man will see his destruction; he will drink the grievous wrath of the Immortal.
Why then does he still take delight in his own house, which he must leave, so that his life is cut short and broken off midway?
Who will teach God Most High, so that he may know?
For he indeed judges the cases of the lofty men.
One man dies in the midst of his youth, at its prime, and he has the bloom of young manhood, when his strength is greatest;
Prosperous, flourishing on both sides, and at peace, and he fears nothing;
But his soul, flying from his limbs, had gone to Hades, lamenting its fate, leaving behind its vigor and its youth.
In the season of his prime, when the marrow moistens his bones, in the spring season, when milk fills the vessels;
But he, having a cruel spirit and being dishonored, perishes away from life, and never having eaten a sweet-tasting morsel.
But alike in the dust all shall lie down to sleep, and in one honor both the wicked and also the noble, until they become spoil and prey for worms.
But I well know the cares of your own heart, and all the helpless things you devise, insulting me.
For you say, Where is the palace of the ruler?
Where is the house with lofty head of the far-famed king?
Where are the halls of the ruler?
and where are their people and city?
In what bosom of the earth do the dwellings of the impious stand (if indeed he lives anywhere)?
where do the wanderers dwell?
Would you not have inquired of these, who, meeting you at the crossroads, accost you, and do you know their proof?
Thus some are not at all safe, but reckless, and only for a little while; and from evils they are saved by some relentless sparing, until deadly fate and the pitiless day arrive.
And presently, called again toward death, they crawl, just as from a prison, and for them destruction is sheer and steep, on the day when the visitation and wrath of God come to be.
But who then will convict the man of his overweening outrage, or who, looking him in the face, will reproach him for his deeds?
Will anyone indeed repay him to his face for all that he has done?

But even so, being such as he is, mighty and without lament, he shall go down into Hades, and among the dead he shall shine forth, Mimnas, in the grave, dwelling in a house in the tomb, where his brothers and kinsmen shall bury him.
There he sleeps softly and in sweet slumber, and he will lie down gladly, and the clods of earth are sweet to him in the valleys;
But we, wretched men, all the tribes of men, are sprinkled upon him, some before and others after;
And around him stand countless feeble heads of the dead, as many as leaves and flowers come to be in season.
But why do you comfort me with these things in vain?
How vain is your consolation, friends, and your folly has been considered in your words.
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and spoke to him, having been stirred up:
for indeed wrath, exceedingly great, held him;
Can a man profit God with his own understanding, as a man who is distinguished in prudent mind?
Is he himself greatly profited or benefited by his prudence?
What delight is this to God, if you were righteous?

Or what great profit to him are your pure ways, even if you yourself were blameless and knew blameless things? Is it because he fears your punishment and your deadly deeds, that he reproves you, or does something else more shameless? Therefore now he has convicted you, and in justice has stood against you.

lg.l: Ἦ ὅτι σὴν ἀτίτην τρομέει, καὶ λοίγια ἔργα,
Μή τι μιν ὑβρίζῃς, ἢ ἄλλό τι κύντερον ἔρδῃς,
Τούνεκα νῦν σε ἔλεγξε, καὶ ἐν δίκῃ ἀντίος ἔστη;

p.s: Fool, are not your countless offenses, your boundless transgression, and your endless wickedness?
Do not violence and force reach the iron heaven?
For trusting in your tongue and your mighty hands, you recklessly, and not according to order, took your brother as a pledge, pitiless one, and you did not give him any recompense for his toil.
From the naked man you took away his garments, and he had nothing to throw around himself.
To the weary man you did not give water to drink, and you withheld bread from the hungry.
And this is still much more dreadful: that you let the thirsty go without drink, and the hungry without food.
But he took the land, whose power was greatest, and Okeus, who of all men obtained the portion of the most abundant honor for his wife;
But of the others you did not regard them in your mind, nor did you care;
Nor did you ever care for widows, nor did you pity orphans, whose dear parents have died;
But you sent them away empty, and you yourself broke your arm.
Therefore woven snares have encircled you from every side, and about your feet spreading nets are poured out, and sudden trembling and fears confound your spirit;
And darkness poured around, so that you may not see the light of the sun with your eyes, the sweet light of the sun;
And rivers swelling, and a swollen flood made you submerged, and it washed you away with boundless water.
Does God (for so you said) dwell in the highest halls on the topmost peak of wide-gaping Olympus, very far off, where heaven is highest above the earth?
Look at the stars, how for him the lofty peaks stand above the earth;
and God is higher than the stars.
How does God know?
How did you know?
How did he perceive?
Truly, would he perhaps see through the dark clouds?
Or would he discern anything through the misty air?
Is he not quite wrapped in cloud, so that he sees nothing, and he walks far from the earth upon the circle of Olympus?
But will you keep to the ancient path that wicked men trod, and the broad way that men of old walked, which is destroyed?
Who are quickly withered, like flowers altogether out of season.
For when a river in flood had scattered their foundations, and a winter torrent down from the mountains, and a boundless storm had arisen, they collapsed at their very roots and were being destroyed.
Because they have dared to look God in the face, and to mock him with reproachful words: 'Away far from us, Olympian! What need have you of this?'
Come now, go, give way, withdraw far back!

But what more could God do for them that is to their heart's desire, even if he were able to accomplish it, and if it were accomplished? For he gave them boundless wealth in their halls and wondrous riches;
but enough for them;
yet their fields are heavy with fruits, and their houses are filled with good things.
Far from me be the counsels and devices of impious men, since the plan of sinners does not please my heart.

Truly the good man and the children of the good man would have rejoiced, and all the pious would have greatly exulted in their heart, and inextinguishable laughter would have arisen among righteous men, when they saw those suffering through the land because of their follies, and bearing griefs beyond their fate because of their own recklessness.
And thus someone spoke, looking at another nearby: 'Our wealth was not yet being cut down, but the remnant of it all, poured out, was the rush of consuming fire.'
But come, cease from strife, subdue your great-hearted spirit, and do not, Job, wish to contend with the King of Heaven, but rather to bring favor, so that he may be gentle.
Now then, converse with him in friendship, and persuade him, cutting oaths, so that a good portion may be yours, and all things may turn out fittingly.
Receive now from the mouth the life-sustaining law, and quickly the words of life, and cast them into your heart, whose voice flows from the tongue sweeter than honey.
But if you urge your backward-turning step toward the Immortal One, you shall stand securely, subdued as before, and far from your tents you shall cast away wickedness.
You shall store up countless gold like dust, and like the most abundant that lies about the paths in the season of summer.
And you shall heap up gold like dust, and Ophir like pebbles.
And they shall lie abundantly by the fair-flowing rivers.
The Almighty shall be your defense and abundant strength, and gold, which is a great support for mortal men.
You shall have gold and silver in abundance.
Then you shall delight your heart in splendor, lifting your eyes to Olympus, and sweet longing for the Almighty shall possess you, and it shall become a great joy to you.
You will call on him as you pray, and he will swiftly listen to the voice of the one praying, and you will pay your vows.
It will be steadfast, and no word you speak will be in vain.
If you set your mind on anything, this will be accomplished for you.
And around your paths a sweet light will shine.

Whenever the memory of the tribes of overweening mortals fell in the dust, subdued beneath the hands of God, you will say that God, thinking kindly thoughts for you, raised you on high, and gave you to be ever-envied and pre-eminent above others, distinguished among many and outstanding among heroes.
He who easily brings low the man who trusts in his own speechlessness, and will save the man adorned with gentle reverence.
Often blameless inhabitants rescued their native land from fate by their judgments and by their own counsel.
And now you might ward off the hateful ruin from the island by your beneficence and the purity of your hands.
Then noble Job, groaning greatly, answered him: 'Woe is me, that now my form has become unseemly, as I lament over ceaseless pains.'
Even if I groan sorely and shed countless tears, yet my wound has become sorer than my groaning.
I do not shed as many tears as the grief for which they are worthy.
Would that I might find God and reach his throne, as I wish I could stand upon the divine threshold.
Would that I might be set face to face in judgment, so that I might know his ordinance.
I would dare to set it out before him, and to face his reproaches, and his upright words; and I will take up the contest of his speeches, a tongue well-fenced with refutations and steadfast words.
Ah, then I would know the words he would speak to me; I would consider in my heart what he might say against me.
Would he indeed contend with me in his great strength, he who is a poor man, trusting in his might, relying on hands and valor?
(Ah me, since no one could match his strength) — Not indeed...
But he will put into my breast a very bold, fearless spirit, increasing my strength beyond envy.
There the righteous would judge him duly, eagerly, in their desire that the arbiter grasp the outcome.
And I would hope to win victory and glory from God, who has spoken judgment most uprightly among all.
But woe is me, wretched, since God is unseen;
I went forward, but I did not see him;
and backward, but not even so am I able to see him with my eyes.
Whether I go to the right toward the dawn and the sun, or I go to the left toward the misty darkness;
I have not seen him on the left, where he wrought dreadful things;
nor on the right, for there he is hidden.
But nevertheless that one has clearly known my paths;

Grieved at all things, he saw my ways and knew my mind; for he tested me as in the furnace of misery, and I come forth like gold that shines greatly, which gleams brightly when purified in the flame of fire.
Firmly I pursued his track with my feet; I kept to the straight-going traces of his paths, and with unwavering feet, and I did not miss the road.
Nor did my heart, blameless, shrink from the commandments which the Father enjoined, but he set a holy ordinance from it;

As a treasure in the bosom, whatever came from him through the mouth, this is more precious to me than a portion of food, which it befits me to receive, or a portion of food, and barley, the marrow of men.
But there is no man who has fitted himself to divine things by diminishing them;
Nor will anyone make void what God in his own mind intends, nor make it idle;
His mind is one and the same, and his counsel is one;
He has done whatever he wishes, and it was dear to his heart.
This he has accomplished, which was appointed for me;
Indeed many such things are with him, and also others besides.
Therefore trembling seized me, as I looked upon his face;
As I saw, so I shuddered; fear held me as I gazed.
For truly God has loosed my heart within my breast, and with tears and groaning and griefs he has melted my spirit;
The Immortal One has troubled me, he who is mightiest power.
Because I have not perished before these deeds came to be — at once, before the black cloud of misery came upon me, and I saw with my eyes the hateful mist of ruin.

Why is it, since the Immortal well knew all the seasons, both the portion and the portionless lot of mortal men, that nevertheless the evil day, in which the faithless transgressor is about to fall, a man has not known in his heart, nor understood, nor even if one knows God and reveres him in his spirit?
One man moves boundary stones in a rich man's field, and another drives off by force and pastures others' flocks.
Others drove off the orphan's donkey, and there was no longer any mercy, and they took in pledge the cattle of blameless widows.
And yielding to violence and grievous transgression, they thrust aside the wayfarers who were worn down by poverty.
But the poor are hidden alike beneath the recesses of the earth, from those who do violence to them;
For pale fear seized them greatly.

And they went out raging after their own wicked deeds, having in their breasts a pitiless and savage heart, like wild asses, which in the desert rush out from their caves at the appearing of dawn, in case they might find some prey that would be after their own heart;
And the desert gave them food and to their children.
Such arrogant and violent men, wanton outlaws, wandered over the blooming plains and the rich works of men, eating another's livelihood unpunished;
They plundered their possessions, and drove off much plunder.
They came to another's deep-corned field, and they came holding sharp sickles in their hands;
They came to a fair vineyard heavy with grapes, not their own;
and the clusters upon them were dark;
And they, gathering it by force, held the honey-sweet fruit.
Whoever was naked, with no rag to throw around him, they sent him away all night long, unclad, in the season of winter.

But the rain soaked him, when the rushing water flows with a roar down the mountains, raging with a dark whirlwind; who, when he has found shelter from the cold away from others, sleeps under a hollow rock, under the shelter of the north wind; and he clings fast to it, so that it may be a covering for him from the wind.

And when you stretch out your loving hands to an orphan child, smiling sweetly at him in his grievous infancy, they snatch him from the breast and from the bosom of his nurse, having a pitiless heart;
and they have stripped the poor man bare;
And they give him no rag to cover him, and they send him out naked, and let him go naked.

Those whose dear limbs had been loosed by grievous famine and by toil, and who never found life-sustaining handfuls of grain, but were plunderers, so that they might not even have enjoyment of gleanings.

They gather shining olives in the threshing floors, and tread the grapes at the wine-vats dear to unmixed wine, gaining wages for themselves and their child, yet never, though drinking, did they put away their parching thirst.
There together arose the wailing and the cry of men both dying and perishing.
And the earth flowed with blood;
The violence and force of those who struck the iron heaven with the sword reached up, and your plundering was not unseemly, O Cappolis, as you trampled;
And an unceasing din had arisen.
But God was soon about to punish the guilty one, and not with impieties, he would permit these deeds to be understood.
Wretched men know from where the light is, nor where the dawn is, nor where the sun that shines on mortals goes over the earth, wrapped in mist and cloud;
Nor does the shining Sun ever look upon them with his rays, nor when he goes toward the starry heaven, nor when he turns back again to the earth from heaven.
But deadly night is spread out over wretched mortals.

Man, man, bane of mortals, murderer, stormer of walls, you too before the sun, before the undying dawn appears, rise from your bed to slay a needy man, and like a thief you wander in the dead of night.

The adulterer, wandering by night, rolled his deceitful eyes, and sat waiting in the halls until the bright eye of heaven should sink, and the friendly evening star should come, dragging black night over the life-giving earth.
But when darkness comes, and all the streets are scattered abroad, he says that no eye, however sharp, shall see him; for he prayed to be covered by such a cloud.
Others indeed (for the arts of evil are full of devices;

But I would not tell of them all, nor name them, not even if I had ten tongues and ten mouths, which through the murky night bored through the chambers, all that before, along with the day, they chose as spoil to diminish.
They do not love the light, and the desire of darkness seizes them.
The gloomy night came upon them all, most longed for.
Truly for others the dawn brought light that gladdens mortals, but for these it is hateful, like the black shadow of death.
But if anyone should see with his eyes, or learn of deeds, then in that way the dark cloud of death covered them, and murky fear gave over their dark-encircled minds.
They were terribly afraid, and they shrank back.
As when someone, seeing a serpent, starts back and stands away in the glens of a mountain, and trembling seizes his limbs;
Thus they shuddered, whenever anyone might look upon them.
And they, terribly frightened, each thought of flight, swift as rushing waters that flow quickly.
But their allotted portion of wealth and all their possessions upon the earth, as much as they had before, a wicked touch destroyed, and it crushed them, and the smiting Fury scattered them at once.
But they wander solitary, apart from others; they do not go in among mortals, nor do they openly work the fat fields, nor yet the unplowed ground of flourishing vineyards.
As cold snow, which from water is ice, drought and heat, so the grave has seized the wicked man;

The womb that bore him shall forget him; of him, even though he is dead and laid in the dust, worms shall make a rich feast in his inward parts, devouring his fat, cutting away what lies upon the surface.
He has perished, so that not even his name is left among men, nor shall he have a memorial among later generations.
Transgression breaks forth, like a boar, until in the mountains both the East Wind and the South Wind fell upon it, and the blustering West Wind too;
And they hurled their long-pointed branches at one another with a wondrous roar, and there was a crashing of them as they were shattered.

But she was a barren woman, and not knowing of childbirth; him, then, having rushed on with violence, the wretched one, ever sinful, kept wearing down with a witless spirit, and kept insulting the widow, and kept doing many evils, as many as all the others did not.
He drags them off by his mighty strength;
as he rose up, no one any longer trusts that he still lives among the living, but he hoped that then it was fated for him to be caught by loathsome death, since he raged no longer bearably.

If God granted him to be safe and not to perish, both at ease for a little while and unharmed, alive — yet even afterward he would pay for his wanton and cruel deeds, glaring fiercely, stretching a very vengeful eye.
For a little while they are lifted up, and the impious are still superior to all; but presently again they were dashed down in the dust.

They are gone, just like all the other mortals who are upon the earth, utterly swept away, nameless among men, inglorious they have died, and God has taken away their glory — as when one cuts off the topmost heads of the ears of grain.
But if this is not true, as I declare, then who will reproach me for my speech, as many companions as there are?
Or will he speak again?
Who among you will convict me of falsehood, and show plainly that I do not speak with understanding?
Then Bildad the Shuhite, greatly angered, answered him:

The king of Olympus, who dwells in the highest halls, holds sway over all with his might, and rules over all, and is a lord and high-counsellor, and a deviser of fear, and sits alone unmoved upon lofty thrones, and under peace governs the whole host of the heavenly ones.
Is there then any number of the heavenly hosts?
Or is there anyone on the earth on whom God has not sent down from heaven sweet light and lovely radiance?
How could a wretched man be holy before God, one who is mortal and whose mother bore him mortal?
If you know God, how is he blameless in justice?
But look at all the stars, with which heaven is crowned;
The stars are bright, and the moon is radiant;
So it seems to us mortals;
In the eyes of God the stars are not bright, nor is the gleaming moon;
For many things, O Job, that seem fair have appeared to him not fair.
How is a man, who is a wretched worm, made?
Is he a child of man, who is a wretched worm made?
Then much-enduring noble Job answered him:
Oh wow, truly a very clever man and a clear-voiced speaker!
How you have helped a weak man with your words, and one of little strength, who has no might nor any defense!
By your counsels have you put in strength and might?
How you would be a counselor among the foolish, and would weave for them a defense against evil and a blameless counsel!
How you have now recounted the whole truth very fully!
And to whom do you say these things?
Whose spirit, then, do you keep alive, once it has been breathed out?
Who revived, once he heard your word?
For I too clearly know that fear from him is to be appeased;
Nor then does he abide only above, in the aether and the clouds, but also below, in the waters and the sea, he rules over all;
The dead who have died, who dwell in the deepest depths of the barren sea, were driven back again beneath the waters by his will.
For him the recesses of Hades and the dreadful dwellings have been revealed, grim, dank, which even others loathe.
Easily do the ever-gleaming Furies appear to him from Erebus among the dead, and broad Tartarus gaped open.

Straightway the gates of the baleful pit bellowed, and the lord of the dead below, Aidoneus, shuddered; and in fear he leapt from his throne and cried out, lest the Father of men and gods should break open the earth above him.
He who stretched out the north over the void, hanging the earth upon nothing, so that it stood self-founded, yea, firmly fitted throughout by its weights.
He bound the waters in his thick clouds, and the cloud was never burst though it weighs heavily, bearing so great a burden in its pregnant bosom.
He covered the shining eye of the wondrous deep, he spread a cloud over the throne which he did not veil, upon it.
He covered the air thickly, and Olympus grew dark.

He who also ran around the shore with the great sea, and set a fence with the waves, which it is not lawful to pass by, until day yields to night and night to day, and light and darkness bring a lovely exchange.
The starry vault was shaken, and the topmost pillars of Heaven were astonished, trembling at his morning threat.
He split the sea with mighty force here and there, and smote it with overweening pride, trusting in his utterly foolish mind.
He adorned the upper air with the many cunning devices of his mind, and the sky with the fair-seeming embroideries of stars;
A dread serpent, a great portent, a monster, a wonder to behold, crooked, many-coiled, he fashioned with his own hands.
And these are but the edges of God's works;
but he is mightier than report;
How small a portion of him do we hear of!
Dread is the thunder when it crashes from heaven; who can clearly know what the thunderbolt of his divinity would accomplish?
Truly he groaned heavily, and Job ceased from his speeches; and again he took up his word, and spoke a word, and swore an oath:

By the life of God, who imperishable, undying, forever holds strength everlasting, and can accomplish all things, who destroyed my life and took away my noble mind, and put a bitter thought in my breast — never, as long as I live and have life-sustaining breath, and while a divine blast remains in my nostrils, will anyone hear from me a wicked word, or a reckless one, nor will transgression pass back through the fence of my teeth; I will not deceive anyone's mind with thievish words, nor ever beguile with flatteries of the tongue.

lg.l: Οὔποθ’, ἕως ζώω, καὶ ἔχω ζωαρκέα πνοιὴν,
Καί μοι θεσπεσίη μίμνει ἐν ῥίνεσσιν ἀϋτμὴ,
Οὔ τις ἀκούσει ἐμεῖο κακὸν ἔπος, οὐδ’ ἀσύφηλον,
Οὐδέ τ’ ἀτασθαλίη μοι ἀμείψεται ἕρκος ὀδόντων,
Οὔτινα κλεψινόοισι παραπλάγξω φρένα μύθοις,
Οὐδέ ποτε γλώσσης μειλίγμασιν ἠπεροπεύσω.

p.s: Nor will I justify you;
may this not happen;
Nor will I cast away my innocence of hands, until I die and the fated day comes upon me;
But I hold fast to righteousness, and I will not let it go;
My heart will not be shaken by secret reproaches;
As long as I still live and see the light of the sun.
But whoever hates me, and knows no friendly designs, and rises up against me with hostile intent, devising evils — let an equal fate befall him and the reckless man.
For what hope is there for the crooked-minded deceiver?

Even if his wealth were ten times and twenty times as much as all that he now has, and if more should come from somewhere, would his great wealth avail him anything on that day when the Lord takes away from him his honey-sweet life?
Will God, being well-disposed, listen favorably when he supplicates him?
Will he greatly propitiate the ears with his own prayers, when hateful ruin and dread distress come upon him?
Will God indeed be a great joy to him, and in whom he has trusted, will he delight his heart and take pleasure all his days?
Or will he as a suppliant pray to him with unceasing voice forever?
But I will gladly instruct you, and I will not conceal, how many glorious works of God, and the wonders he wrought long ago with his hands, I will show—the treasures of his divine counsel.
But if you know clearly, and see with your eyes how all things have come to be (since you are not ignorant), why do you still contend with your friend with vain words?
This indeed was the portion of the wicked, and the appointed fate, and this honor from heaven did proud men receive, who oppress others, holding overweening insolence.

If any of them was adorned in his bed with dear gifts, and was also blessed with many children, yet nonetheless she bore sons doomed to a wretched fate, and as such a mother bore these short-lived ones;

For either in war, subdued beneath the hands of foes, they have been struck by the two-edged sword, and were destroyed, or else (which is the most pitiable death for wretched mortals) they have died of famine, since they lacked food.
And if any of his survivors be left among the few-born, he shall go down to the grave unwept, nor shall widows wail shrilly around him with bereaved women.
And thus shall some woman speak, and lead the lamentation: Woe is me, wretched woman, woe is me, ill-fated in my noble offspring.

If he gathers silver past telling, like dust, and cloaks and tunics, and well-spun rugs, and a countless multitude of clothing, like clay, which in all the streets is ever poured out in boundless abundance—
Whatever he may prepare, the toil shall be bootless;
Nor shall so many talents of silver avail him, nor so many fine garments;
For God, having taken away his wealth, will give all these things to upright men to divide.

All the beautiful, golden, gleaming houses that had been built for him with splendors — and they seem to him to be imperishable — yet these are feeble, like a moth's dwelling, or like a shepherd's fold, and short-lived, which he perhaps soon spoke of under a little wind's blast.
The rich man lay down, and his great wealth rushed away;
He was roused from sleep, and nothing more was told him; he opened his eyes, and saw nothing further.
Evening left him rich; dawn found him poor.
Terrors in succession seized him, one after another, like the long waves of the loud-roaring sea, and evil storms snatched him away through the night.
The East wind, rushing upon him, snatched him away (he is gone himself), and hurled him far off, raging with a dark tempest.
And God will cast many grievous things upon him, and will not pity him; it would be welcome to him to escape from his hands.
In the assembly of men the clapping of hands ever rose up against him in unseemly fashion, and while many were hissing, shame and modesty stole him away from his seat.
Silver has a mine beneath the earth, where it is dug out, and gold has a place, which later in time a craftsman works with skilled mind.
From the mother earth came iron, a deadly offspring; from stone drawn out, bronze is smelted in fire.

For a mortal man, by the deep cunning of his mind, went into the subterranean recesses, and plunged into the dread, murky depths of the earth, and cast light in the shafts, seeking treasures and gathering up everything precious, whether steel, or the offspring of bronze, or the seeds of gold.
And precious stones beneath, and all metals out of the dread hollow, and out of the deep sand (of which you might say they are in the black shadow of death, whoever dug them;
so wide did the earth gape) he brought them forth to the light, and they saw the sunbeams with the sun.

If ever suddenly water flowed from within a pit, gushing upward, (and the waters of the earth swelled), and if otherwise, driven among the mountains by God's rain, a torrent rushed forth, and in such a way that it is a support for both feet, and it diminishes the works of men;

There a man skilled in channeling turned the mouths of rivers now this way, now that, expertly guiding the stream of water, holding a mattock in his hands, and casting out the refuse of the channel, or through pipes;
And it, flowing swiftly, murmurs — a wave rushing back again — and it even outruns the one who leads it.
Our dear earth is a nourisher of bread, and beneath its belly a fire hidden within is stirred up.
Stones are the seat of sapphires beneath the bosoms of Mother Earth, who holds gold-rich dust in her belly.
There is a path which no bird has ever seen, nor has the vulture beheld it with its eyes, which they say is the sharpest-sighted of the birds above.
That path the cubs of the tawny lion have not known, nor does the grim lion tread it with his terrible feet.
But a man thirsting for the treasures of the earth has trodden it.

He, when he hoped for a treasure being beneath, smote the rocks, trusting in force and hands; he struck the rocks, and overturned the heads of the lofty mountains, and they from the root were dashed down headlong with a rush, and the depths surged up.
Among the midst of the crags a river of deep-eddying waters he dug out; every precious thing his eye has seen.
He checks the grievous streams of overflowing rivers;
a great wave he holds back, and it leaps over the bank.
If anything has been hidden away, he quickly brought it to light.
Where then can one, seeking wisdom, find it?
Or where is the place of lovely understanding?
For no one of earth-dwelling men ever saw how honored it is, and worthy of all others.
It is not findable by a mortal, nor does it attend the living.
"It is not in me," said the deep, firmly refusing; "It is not with me," said the sea, strongly denying.
No one can buy it with gold, nor give it in exchange, nor ever with silver, even if he should bring countless purchase-price.
For neither of the two could be weighed equal in wisdom, nor if one should give as much as sand and dust, nor even ten times and twenty-times-counted gifts.
Gold of Ophir is far unworthy of her, nor is the value of onyx and sapphire so great.
With it neither intricately-wrought gold could compare, nor pure crystal;
nor could anyone exchange it for fair stones of highly-honored gold.
Nor shall there be any mention of red coral, or of pearls shining afar;
nor in account, nor in number;
But this is better than all pearls — a godlike mind, and a prudent understanding, and a wise-hearted spirit.
Not so worthy is the yellow topaz, which even from the Ethiopians who dwell afar has been brought hither;
Pure gold that existed before, and much refined gold, is not equal to it, since it has never obtained a like honor.
Therefore, from where has wisdom come, the queenly mother?
Or indeed, what place is there of lovely self-restraint?
Because it has easily escaped the eye of every living being and of one that looks upon the earth, and it has eluded sight;
It is not yet unseen by the birds of the sky, whose eye also looks out most sharply from its head.
Destiny and death, twins, have denied it, and having one spirit they cried out with a concordant voice: 'We indeed hear only a rumor, and we know nothing.'
But God understands the way, and he knows the place; where wisdom abides he clearly knows, and where she dwells.
For he gazes everywhere to the farthest ends of his earth, and from heaven afar he stretches his all-seeing eye.

When he made the swift paths of the blustering winds, so that they are dashed with a roaring beneath the clouds, he set in a balance the heavy-breathing blasts, and weighed them, and gave measure to the waters well and skillfully, and with a plumb-line he directed the sea, so that its stream might flow, and not rush upon the dry land;

(For if the bounds of these things had not been fitted according to order, all things would at once have been confounded, and the sea would have mingled with the upper air.) And he set a boundless ordinance for the streams of rain, so that the fields might be drenched enough with thick drops.
And with thunder and lightning he drove a wondrous path, so that with a dreadful crash the din might arise throughout Olympus, through the cloud of the lightning-flashing fire of God.
When God first adorned all these things, then he beheld it, and with his own spirit pondered it, discerning well, and having searched it out he cut it off.
And he said to the man:
Behold, wisdom is the fear of God, and to shun evil is understanding, lovely.
Thus he spoke;
And then he addressed his companions with a word, but they became silent;
and again he spoke a word;
Would that I were in my youth, and my strength were steadfast, as in former months and days, when God stood by me in all my labors, and guarded me.
By his light, when torches shone around my head, a wondrous radiance guided my path through the darkness, and I walked safely through the long gloom.
As when the most lovely flower of youth was upon me, the counsel of the Immortal One waited about my tents.
As in former days, while God was still with me, and my children around me.
As when my every footstep was washed with butter, with sweet oil, and the rock poured out for me streams of honey-sweet olive oil.
Whenever I rose up and went to the gate, or came through the city, or set my seat in the street.
As they saw me, so at once they hid themselves, the vigorous young men, and they did not dare to remain, but shrank from my face, and awe seized them.
And the elders rose up at once, and they stood still when they looked at me, and reverence held each man.
Mighty kings fell silent in stillness, yielding to shame, and they feared to speak to me while I was present, laying their hand upon their mouth.
Therefore the glorious leaders stood speechless, and their tongue stuck to their silent throat.

When an ear heard my voice, it blessed me; and when one heard me speak, he would say this: 'O blessed Job, born to destiny, happy and fortunate, thrice-blessed are your father and your honored mother, and most blessed the womb that bore you.'
as one spoke a word in wonder, when he heard him speaking.
And an eye has seen me, and it was a witness for me: how I saved justice for the poor, and heard their prayers, at once for the choking man, and warding off the violence of the overbearing.
As a father to the aged, and a guardian of the orphan, and I readily defended him, so that I was a helper to him.
Whoever was faint of strength, and destruction was near him, he prayed stretching out his hand, and earnestly beseeching me much: I beseech you, lord, and I pray to be your suppliant.
May God give you as much as you desire in your heart.
So he spoke praying, and God also heard his voice.
Long did the widow's heart laugh with gladness as she murmured, for I was such a helper to her.
I was clothed in righteousness as in a cloak, and my good order was like a diadem and a garment.
I was eyes to the blind, and a foot to the lame.
Always to the poor, like a father, I was gentle; I would break up their cases, whenever strife had arisen among men, so that I might discern both the evil and the good.
I smashed the jaws of the monstrous ruffian, and snatched the sweet prey out of the midst of his teeth.

Then I said, trusting in feasting and peace, unshaken and at rest I shall die in my nest; in my own house I sit on a seat in old age, my days are as countless as sand and dust; and my root spread beside the fair streams, and all night long my branch held its flourishing dew.

lg.l: Ῥίζα δέ μοι καλοῖσιν ἐπίλνατο ἀμφὶ ῥεέθροις,
Παννυχίην τ' ἐμὸν ἔρνος ἔχεν τεθαλυῖαν ἐέρσην.

p.s: Always my good glory flourished among men;
My great rounded bow, which was fitted to my hands, remained steadfast, as if newly made, always; but it was stretched out, trusting in both the bow and in strength.
When I spoke, people listened to me greatly and obeyed, waiting in silence, until I myself should appear, eager to hear my blameless counsel.
As I spoke, whatever my heart within my breast urged me, they did not come to pass without effect, and no one spoke against me, (for shame came upon them) and no one addressed me with a word.
My speech dripped upon them like dew, and from my tongue flowed a voice sweeter than honey.
As when a thirsty threshing-floor awaited the autumn rain, and the parched earth gaped for the late-falling rain, so they stood with mouths open, until I poured sweet speech from my melodious throat.
If ever I smiled, laughter creased my face, but they would not believe it, for before now they still thronged to me, though I was fearsome and august to behold among men.
But so that my eyes were not darkened with gloom.
Nor did reproach draw near, but very brightly it flew cloudless, and a white radiance ran over it.
As a king was greatly preeminent among hosts, a leader (for he stands out among spear-fighting men), and he charmed the mind of those who mourned, and stirred their spirit.
How God made me ever-envied on that day, distinguished among many and preeminent among heroes, ever sung of, a great leader of peoples.
Such was I formerly, at once honored and dear, and like a god honored among all mortals.
Woe is me! Now again all things are turned about.
But now I am greatly a laughingstock and a plaything to the younger men, whose fathers I would have disdained to set with my dogs, to guard the fair-fleeced flocks.
For never did those who were mighty profit me.
Whether in word, or in deed, or with hands, or by force, their life has perished as the circling years roll round, all in vain, ingloriously, and they were worn away by wretched old age.
They who, in poverty and famine, their heart worn with grief, solitary wanderers, roamed through the barren land, and over the desolate plain, straying hither and thither.
Truly, it always appeared rocky and wretched, the land.
(For there is nothing worse for mortals than wandering.
But they, because of their accursed belly, having wretched sorrows, were driven wandering, since ruin and misery and pain came upon them;
They plucked mallow among the bushes (for wretched hunger compelled them), gathering from the midst of thorny thickets, and the root of saltwort, so that it might be food for them.
From among men, as worthless fugitives, they were driven far away, banished from the company;
And mortals went shouting after them, as after a robber.
But then they dwelt in secret in the glens, and in the clefts of the earth, in the hollows, where the deepest recess was, in hollow caves and in deep rocks.
Among the thick bushes they brayed like donkeys, being worn down by hunger, and they were gathered together under nettles.

They themselves are children wholly like their senseless fathers, and their parents were nameless among men, more worthless and lowlier than the earth itself, which ever groans being pressed beneath their feet.
But now they mock me, though I was such a one before, and though they are such as I was, with reproachful words; some of them attack me, and I am held in dishonor.
They loathe me dreadfully, and they stand far off from me; and (a thing that is shameful even for men to hear) they do not respect my face, spitting at me.

Because God has loosed the sinew of my bow, and has bound me with the cords of death and heavy ruin, therefore, urged on by shameless acts, like horses that have broken their tethers and shaken off their harness.

On my right the young men rose up to stand against me, mere infant boys who still breathe their nurse's milk; they tripped me up, so that I might fall in the dust, and they blocked my paths with ruin, as if to meet disaster.
They tripped my footsteps and thrust aside my path; they ruined my roads, and there is no standing firm.
They hasten my ruin, pressing on in wickedness, and though they are trusted friends, no helper attends them.
With all their force they rushed upon me to break down my door, as when a swelling river comes down to the plain in winter-torrent, which flowing swiftly has shattered bridges.
Around me, rolling like a swelling wave, they have come on a murky day, when grievous misery came upon me.
Terrors from every side rushed upon me, one after another, and chased my soul, and shook my dear heart, as a rushing wind shakes a heap on the shore;
violent;
my swift-fated prosperity will pass away like a cloud, which the force of the wind easily scattered.
But now my soul is poured out like water, and hateful ruin and a pitiless day have seized me.
My bones, pierced by nightly pains, ache; my sinews have rotted, and there is no respite from evil.
But violent disease and a bloody weal defiled my garments; and my tunic all around my limbs was bespattered with gore, and with blood, and with dust.
Disease gripped me on every side more than before eating.
He cast me into the mire, the Blameless One, and I was defiled; and black ashes settled upon my shameful limbs, and my skin was dusted over.
I am wholly ashes, and dust.
To you, O Lord, I cried out, but you do not hear the one crying;
Looking toward you I have stood, but you are not one to answer equally.
You have become harsh and savage toward me, and not gentle-minded;
And hostile against me was the strength of your hands.
With a wondrous hurricane you snatched me up, and I am raised on high, having mounted the chariot of the swift-whirling storm.
And you loosed my limbs, and shook apart all my joints.
For I know this well in my mind and in my heart, that you will soon carry me to the all-receiving house of death, where it is fated for all the living to sleep.
And I say he has obtained a share of men.

But surely not even a father will stretch out his hands over a tomb, so as to release the dead from ill-sounding death, even if, in their lives, men in dread affliction each prayed greatly with outstretched hands.
Did not my dear heart lament for a wretched man, groaning over the fate that steep doom came upon him?
Did I not weep for the poor man and suffer griefs in my heart?
Did not pity seize me, when I saw someone wearing evil garments on his body, worn down by hunger, as I looked on?
But though I was ever so gentle and mild, when I hoped good would be present for me, evil came; when I awaited light for us, darkness came.
But my inward parts boiled within me, and a fire blazed deep in my heart.
And there was no relief from my dark sorrows.
But a mournful day of misery came upon me suddenly.
Always, grieving in my breast with a dear heart, I crawl and wander through the misty gloom, and I do not yet see the sweet light of the sun.
And standing in the crowd of men he bellowed a groanless cry.
As I became a brother to serpents, a companion to ostriches and to night-owls.
But my skin is darker around my limbs, like pitch.
And my bones burn with the heat of a fiery disease.
For now my mourning is a song, and my lament was a sweet singing before;
All these things have now left me, both song and lyre;
Instead of the clear-toned lyre I delight always in wailing, and in groaning and tearful weeping.
I made a covenant with my eyes that I should be modest, and never a peeper after maidens;
Why then did a maiden with glancing eyes weigh upon my mind?
For what doom comes from heaven?
Or what appointed fate?
Or what portion came by the will of the great God?
Or what lot was it that came from the high aether?
Is not sheer destruction for men who act recklessly?
Is it not a strange doom for those who devise wickedness?
Did not God then behold my ways, and all my works, and did he not well perceive my footsteps, and with what mind he reckoned them?
If I walked in a slippery path of grievous folly, and rushed into evil deceit with eager heart, and with swift feet, knowing deadly counsels—
Let someone weigh me well in a just balance, and God will know my purity, which attends me.
If I have turned my foot aside from the straight road, and if my heart has gone after the glances of my eye, and if any blame has been upon me, and it has defiled my hands—
Then let me sow, and let another eat the fruit; let even my offspring be rooted out from the root, which I may plant.
If ever the beauty of a mind-charming woman deceived me, if ever I was led astray in my heart by love-breeding words, if I lay in wait with a treacherous ambush at the door of my neighbor—
Then let my wife, shaming my bed and couch, grind for another, having secretly mingled in love;
And let others, having seized my wife, hold her in their arms.
For truly these would be monstrous deeds, and all the many things that judges punish, as is fitting, who guard the ordinances before God;
since they are no longer bearable.
As when a consuming fire falls upon a woodless forest, and the wind drives it, whirling it everywhere, and the bushes fall root-and-branch, urged on by the onset of the fire;
So now would this transgression long ago have cut off my goods, and would have utterly destroyed my root-and-branch prosperity miserably.
If ever I set aside justice, and if I ever shrank from reproach of a male slave or a female slave, when they brought a quarrel against me;
But what shall I do, when the Blameless One rises up against us, and that One who rules mightily over all lawgivers, who is overseer and inspector of all transgressions?
What shall I recount first, what next, and what last?
Did not the One who made me in the womb also fashion him himself?
Did not one craftsman shape for both an equal frame, from mother earth, of the same womb, and from dust?
If ever I took up an unfulfilled desire for the poor, when I was the one giving, and no gentle pity died in me;
If I ever gloated over a wretched widow, and my eyes grew dim and my cheeks were wet with tears;
If I ever ate alone, and alone ate my bread from an inhospitable table, and did not call the orphan to my meal, so that he might share my dinner;
Caring for both, the widow and the orphan, I from childhood reared and cherished the one, embracing him as though he were my own son, and to the other I was a helper from the time my mother bore me;

If I saw a poor man perishing with cold, lacking strength, on the day when the snow thickened the fields, drenched without a cloak and a wind-defending tunic, and never was there for him a rag as shelter against the one wind, nor any defense against the grievous winter;
But he, standing beside me, kept trembling and shivering, and a chattering came through the mouth of my teeth, pale from the chill — and that was the most pitiable thing to see.
If ever I saw such a one frozen to death by the cold.

Rather, whose loins I warmed under the fleeces of my sheep, and who was warmed wrapped in the wool of my sheep, and whose back was made warm, and he would pray, lifting up his hands, 'Hail, lord, because for you, remaining alive, I owe a life-debt.'

If ever I raised my hand against an orphan child with a strong hand, having taken courage, because a just man was dear to me, sitting in the gates, and he came near as a helper, who would soon judge crooked judgments on my account—
Then may my sinews be torn loose from around my shoulder.
May my arm fall entirely, even from the socket, in the dust, from the bones, with the collarbones being broken.
For a grievous and horrible fate appeared to me, which God has sent upon insolent and overweening men; but I cannot endure it, since it was the uttermost.
If ever I gave, trusting in wealth and many possessions, if I relied on beaten gold and refined gold, and said to it, 'You are my hope, and stay, and defense';
If I rejoiced, and my heart was glad within my breast, because I was rich, and wealth flowed to me in abundance;
If I have looked upon the great light of the shining sun, or the gleaming eye of the night-running moon;
And a spirit led me astray in secret against my understanding, and my hand kissed my mouth, and I honored it as a god, as a star;
These too are wicked deeds, and no longer tolerable to a judge, for thus would I have denied the high-ruling God.
But if my heart was warmed at a man's destruction, as he greatly hated me, and I was stirred up at his being in misery;
(For it is not a holy thing for a cowardly mortal to pray.

Nor did my mouth, blind to harm, curse that soul-destroying man with many words, nor did it call down hateful Furies) But if my own household did not speak thus, 'Ah, would that seizing his flesh and rich fat we might have devoured it raw, since no satiety is made for us.'

lg.l: Εἰ δ' οὐχ ἡμέτεροί περ ἐφέστιοι ὣς ἀγόρευον,
"Αἴθ' ἄρ' ἔ μάρψαντες σάρκας καὶ πίονα δημὸν
"Ὦμον βεβρώθοιμεν, ὅτ' οὐ κόρος ἄμμι τέτυκται.

p.s: No stranger used to lodge in the open in the streets, but I opened my doors, that I might receive a wayfaring man.
But if I covered over my transgressions like Adam, hiding my wickedness in my bosom,
Did a great multitude of people truly terrify me?
Or did the tribes of mortals wound my heart with reproaches, so that I sat silent in my house grieving, and did not go out the door, struck by dread terrible fear?
O that someone would press a hearing ear to me! Behold, let God answer me face to face, and I would wish it — this has long been my desire:
O that my adversary would write a truthful book!
Carrying it on my shoulder I would bear it as a lovely burden, or I would set it like a crown upon my temples.
I would declare to him all my steps, and I would count them; I would approach him as a prince.
If my fertile field has reproached me with outrage — verily, and the much-groaning furrows of the land have ceased from their lord — as though I had violently seized another's plot of ground;
If I ate the honey-sweet fruit of the field without paying, or, as one who sacrifices without smoke, gave not even a worthy price, and the Mestians' destruction — those who possessed it before —
Let the earth bring forth thistles instead of wheat, and darnel instead of life-nourishing grain.
Thus then, having spoken, Job ceased from his words.

And so those three all together fell silent, marveling at his speech, for he had spoken very strongly, because in his own mind it seemed to him that he was altogether righteous, and adorned with piety, and not a sinner.
And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, was very angry; indeed he was especially angered at the words which Job had spoken.
For he used to pray that he was pure and blameless in his sight, seeing that he thought himself more righteous than God.
And the three alike were fiercely angry at their companions, because they stood speechless, and they condemned Job, and did not defeat him with opposing words.
And he sat for a long time in silence, waiting until Job should fall silent, and his companions too, because they were older.
But when he perceived one thing at once—three friends listening—for no speech was at hand for them, and he answered a word to Job—he raged relentlessly, and savage anger seized him.
And then indeed he took courage, and answering he spoke a word: 'Hear, friends, and let not each of you be indignant with anger, because I am the youngest in birth among you.'
I am younger in age, but you are elders; therefore I greatly fear, and I did not dare to speak out.
For it is a shame for a young man to speak face to face with an elder.
Truly I said, 'The grey-templed are wise.'
Let the aged speak, and let many days teach, 'How there may be profit, since understanding attends old age,' 'Whoever then was born earlier, he has more already.'
But there is a soul in a mortal, and a divine spirit in his breast, a Thespian breath, giving understanding in his chest.
Not always are men of many years also of much knowledge.
An elder who has grown old might then be a fool in his mind.
And often a younger man might speak with understanding.
Therefore I said, 'And now listen to me, your elder, so that I may say what the spirit in my breast commands.'
Truly I too will show my mind, and I will not conceal it.
Unceasingly awaiting your words, I inclined an ever-listening ear to your speeches, so that you might not speak out, pondering in your minds what I should set forth first, what next, and what last.
But I understood you, and I perceived all things very well, and there was no one among you who refuted Job well with hostile words, and disproved his speech.
It is not so, nor is it fitting for you to speak these things; we know clearly how these deeds come to pass.
To others it is not discoverable by knowledge, but to us alone.
For that man, subdued by the stroke and hand of God, spoke, nor did any cowardly mortal slander him.
For neither did Job speak against me, nor will I answer him with your words, but I will say whatever seemed to me to be better.
Therefore they stood speechless, struck with amazement; truly a great stupor seized each one, and a silence of chilling stupor came to pass.
But when they kept waiting, behold, no one answered Job, but for that reason he sat silent, and did not address him with a word.
Truly I said, 'And I too will answer, as is right.'
Nor shall I be silent, but I will speak, for my spirit urges me to declare it, and I shall go through it all, just as I think.
I am full of words; I bear a pregnant spirit, and I groan, eager to give birth to my words in your presence.

As wineskins are squeezed when stuffed with sweet wine, and it seethes within under a grievous eye, and being pressed it is let out, though longing for a way, and bursting upward it leaps, and soon it has burst from its fullness, and it flows down swiftly and murmurs.
How my heart swells within me as I ponder, my mind boils in my breast, and it breathes all around, eager to break the lid of my lips and the fence of my teeth.
Therefore I will speak out, so that I may breathe a little, open my truthful mouth, and speak plainly.
Let me not now respect the gracious faces of men, nor flatter anyone with soft lies.
For that man is hateful to me, just like the gates of Hades, who hides one thing in his mind but speaks another.
But if I had learned the soothing charms of much-wandering words, bewitching the mind and heart with wily speeches, then he who gave to me before would swiftly have taken away even my life.
For God the Father will not be a helper in support of lies.
Do listen to me, then, Job, and hear my speech; whatever I may now say, lay it up in your heart.
The gates of my mouth were opened, and a voice rushed out; my tongue broke the seal of grievous silence.
I will utter a speech that makes straight, an interpreter of my heart; my lips will recount them very plainly and with constant fitness.
For I too am a mortal, and my lineage is from the same source as yours;
Therefore do not you fear; I too am mortal, a work of the immortal Spirit, a god-fashioned image, such as you also are; and the breath of God he dripped into my nostrils, and breathed in a blast.
Tell me, if you can, and if it is dear to your heart, rouse yourself, good sir, and answer with ready words.
As you said that I wished, and that had long been your desire.
Would that the Lord himself might enter the contest of words, and that he might deign to bring it before you, and I in God's stead—
And do not be afraid of me, since we are one kindred, he who made the others, this one fashioned me well too.
For I too was made a work kneaded in dust, as other mortals are upon the earth eating bread, and my body is molded out of clay.
Therefore I do not question you at all, trusting in my ignorance, nor will I stir you into fear with harsh words, nor — for it is not fitting — will I bring heavy hands upon you.
Take courage, and do not be exceedingly afraid in your heart at all.
I inclined my ear to you, and hearing you speak, truly you have uttered a very arrogant word.
For as you said, 'Truly I am clean and blameless, and knowing what is fitting, and I am no transgressor.'
But there is no ruin in me at all, nor any transgression, since my mind is guileless.
God could easily, if he wished, subdue even an innocent man, and he has found occasion for reproach, so that he might accuse me; he has placed me in the fate of a hostile and wicked man.
He firmly fixed the soles in measured spans; he marked all my footprints and considered where I walk.
And I will tell you another thing, but do you lay it up in your heart:
This you have not spoken well; you resemble a reckless man.
Nor have you spoken according to what is right, for God is mightier than men, by so much also greater in virtue, in honor, and in strength.
Why do you wish to contend with him?
since there is no need at all for you to do so.
For do not, Job, suppose all the words of God—
that you will know;
they will be hard for you, though you are good.
For he did not make his cares plain in his heart, nor does anyone clearly know, as I think, for what reason he did such things;
The Immortal spoke once, and a second time again, but a man has not yet understood in his mind, nor perceived—a fool—nor did he comprehend the voice of him who spoke.
In drowsings, and in visions, in the dead of night, when the tribes of mortals, subdued by soft sleep, slumber very sweetly at the dreamy gates—
There indeed God also instructs mortal men, and very many things he enjoined, and as with a seal he engraved his instruction, so that they might not forget his counsels.
So that he may restrain a man's spirit from his deeds, when he is eager, and may put a stop to him from grievous speechlessness.
At another time, of his own ready will, he warded off wretched destruction from him, and from the sword he rescued his life, his soul from Hades.
And at another time again the Father gave him over to evil, testing him.
So he lies on his bed suffering grievous pains, pierced through all his bones with sharp agonies.
His appetite for drink and food is gone, and no desire for bread and sweet grain seizes his mind, because of his wasting away, and he loathes rich feasting.
But his flesh wastes away in his bending limbs, which formerly were swollen, but now are not seen;
And his bones were dashed, which even before were not seen.
So he, being brought low, because you shoot at a grave with your own mind, said that he was among the living; but already death and mighty fate stand near him.

If indeed there is present with him a messenger, or a prophet, a herald of justice, a witness of good laws, one out of a thousand, and worth as much as many others, who knows in his mind how to speak fitting things, who would show him the path of piety, so that he may be persuaded—
Immediately then the Olympian will be gracious to him, and he will say that he will release him from a fate without grief, because he has found a ransom, and has accepted glorious recompense.
Thus he will find relief from evil, and escape disease; his skin, fresh and smiling with renewed fat, will rejoice in its limbs with splendor, as before.
His sinews and flesh will be more plump than a tender child's, whom his father cherished in great festivity.
