And again he will bloom forth the most graceful flower of youth.
For thus the divine Lord, on account of all the good deeds he has done, will scrape away old age and make him young and in his prime.
He will entreat the Immortal One, and he, knowing gentle gifts, will strike the ever-hearing ear of his prayer;
rejoicing in the divine joy he will look upon his countenance;
Thus he indeed partakes of his own virtue through the good laws of God, he who used to honor justice, and the fitting deeds of pious men, lest anyone being defrauded go away of his equal share.
He watches men, and if any of them has said, "I have sinned, and I have perverted what is right, and it did not profit me, but rather I was harmed more" —
He will rescue his soul, which has gone away from Hades, but he still lives and sees the light of the sun.
Often indeed God has done all these things for a mortal man;
He himself has many good drugs mixed together, and many baneful ones, and with them he might heal the minds of mortals.

So that he might bring back a man's soul again, and give it release, and lead it back up into the light from hateful Hades, and it might rise from the tomb and see the rays of the sun, and still be among the living.
Therefore I will speak to you, and do you give heed, and listen to me; sit in silence quietly, and I will tell you what is fitting.
But if you have any word, answer me, and do not conceal it; speak out whatever you think, and I am willing to be your advocate.
To utter a word as witness of your righteousness.
But if not, you are present in word, listen to my voice; now understand in silence, and I will teach you wisdom.
Indeed he, as Barachiah's blameless son spoke;
Nor did he cease from words any longer, but seeing his companions listening, having drawn himself round in a circle, he spoke winged words:
Hear me, men who are very wise in words, and incline your ears to me, keeping shrewd counsels in your minds.

For his tongue laid out feasts, as it were, full of many turns and very many things, skillfully (for such is the office of the mouth), and from all kinds of food he took tastes, and knew their nature.
As he is both a knower and witness of his own words, whether they are true or not, and whether they are sweet or bitter, already.
But come, let us all be persuaded as I may speak.
Let us weave counsel, and let us consider a plan, so that we may know well what is best to choose.
For Job said exulting, 'I am righteous; God drove out justice from me and stole away my rights.'
Truly, then, shall I speak some falsehood when I judge concerning myself?
But one must not lie, when one knows how to speak clearly.
My wound is relentless, and the pain has become incurable, yet grievous transgression is not the cause for him.
So spoke the loud-boaster, trusting in his speechlessness.
Alas, how then do mortals accuse God?
For from that, they say, they are evil;
but they themselves, by their own recklessness, have sorrows beyond measure.
How there is no other mortal more dream-haunted than Job, who drank reproach and mockery, as when a thirsty man drinks the most gulping water.
Who indeed walked that very road ever among sinful men, and companioned with them, whose concern was reckless deeds.
(As God ever brings like to like.
Again he himself spoke in return about the overweening pride of his mind: 'For not even thus is a man greatly profited, nor is he blamed, who has delighted his dear heart in God.'

lg.l: αὖ πάλιν αὐτὸς ἔφη ὑπεροπλίῃσι νόοιο,
Οὐδὲ γὰρ ὧδ' ἔτω μέγ' ὀφέλλεται, οὐδ' ἐνίνηται
Ἀνήρ, ὅς τε Θεοῖο τετάρπηται φίλον ἦτορ.

p.s: But you also be persuaded, since to obey is better. Hear me in my words, all you who are wise of mind.
The Lord has not yet done evil things, and may this not happen, nor is there any grievous wickedness with the Immortal One.
For to a man he paid a wage worthy of his deeds, and he gave to each, as is right, according to what he did.
Surely God would not, yielding to violence, do wicked things, nor would the Immortal ever pervert justice.
Who then entrusted to him the helm of the crumbling earth?
Who is ruler of the wide-spaced earth, to whom the boundless world, to whom peoples have been entrusted, and all things are a care?

If he sharply perceives a mortal, and takes away his own life, and again gathers to himself both breath and life, then all flesh alike will perish utterly, and men will be dissolved back into dust, whence they were born long ago.

lg.l: Πᾶσ' ἅμα σὰρξ ἀπολεῖται ἐπήτριμος, ἐς δ' κονίην
Ἀνέρες ἂψ λύσονται, ὅθεν πάρος ἐκγεγάασιν.

p.s: If you have an understanding mind in your breast, Job, save yourself, and listen to me, and cast my word into your heart.
Shall he indeed be a ruler, to whom righteous ordinances are not dear, who hates justice, and has he not perished while doing wicked deeds?
Who was most righteous, surpassing all others, and they say he spoke justice most uprightly — and would you dare to judge this one, and to reproach him to his face?
Is it then, in due measure, O lord, that one says, 'You are a wretch and a sinner'?
Are you reckless, you rulers?
For who, being a clear-voiced speaker, would have dared thus to reproach kings with insulting words?
How does it no longer befit God to have spoken these things?
Who rules over all mortals and immortals, who does not respect the august faces of kings, nor has regard for the wealthy;
For the poor man before him is equal to the rich man, and has obtained an equal honor;
For all alike are the work of their hands.

Suddenly he covered them with the end of death together with these, and the tribes of mortals shuddered in the dead of night; and straightway they perish helpless, and the lords, hurled from their seats, took the vast ground with their teeth, subdued not by a mortal but by the blow and hand of God.
For his eyes are upon the ways of men, and being all-seeing, they range over the gates, watching the insolence and the lawfulness of men.
Peering at each one, he saw all the footprints of men.
There is no darkness so great in shadowy chambers below, where the fates of black death dwell apart, that it could wrap around impious men, even if someone wished to do something hidden from God.

If anyone should grieve because of the evils that he has done, and you should punish him unjustly, and God should smite him, yet he has suffered nothing more than is right, so that he may contend with God and come face to face with him in judgment because of this outrage;
for the Fury is most just.
And he smote countless tribes of mighty kings, and cast down the worthless upon lofty thrones.
For thus the Olympian apportions wealth to men, to the good and to the bad, just as he wishes, to each one.

But he well knows their violence and reckless deeds, and down upon them in the middle of the night he cast with heavy hand; and they, being wounded, were left in the dust, prone in the dust they were left, and they perished.

He struck down the openly wicked, where the people were most numerous, so that all might see and tremble at God's visitation; and here let one then say, seeing another near him, 'Evil deeds do not prosper; fate overtakes the sinner; so may another also perish, whoever would do such things.'

Because they turned their footstep away from God, and turned back, and drew far back, and it is no concern to them in their hearts how much he did, and how much he accomplished against them, and they did not heed his commands.
These men insult, and an unquenchable cry of wretched poor arose, whom they wear down with violence, and a certain cry reached heaven and cast down upon God.
The poor man would cry out, and God would hear his prayers.
When he grants calm, who will bring terror?
Who will behold him, when he hides his face, whether when he brings calamity upon many, being angry with men and people, or upon one alone?

He did not allow a deceiver to rule among men (the scepter and the ordinances which he gave to kings), lest a devourer-of-the-people wear down the citizens with evil plots, one who always cares for mischievous deeds, lest the people be entangled in the snares of the treaders, lest haply caught like in a net without a mesh, in an all-catching one, they become spoil and prey for hostile men.
Therefore you must, O Job, say such things to God: "Be gracious to me, O King, and put a gentle spirit in me;
Alas for me, because I suffered many things and toiled much!
No longer will I sin, lest I suffer something worse.
Come then, show me also that which I myself cannot see;
But if ever I erred, trusting in foolish wits, I would no longer go on sinning, and there will be a respite from evil for me.
Is this how it shall be, as is dear to your heart?
But indeed these things lie among the races of God;
For indeed, whether you wish it, you will pay the penalty, or whether you refuse, 'Not I.'
Therefore you too declare whatever you know.
But rather let the prudent and wise, whoever they are, who among mortals are distinguished in their shrewd minds, speak, and let them take heed of my words.
Job is a fool, since he speaks windy nonsense, and he has spoken many things in vain, such as an understanding man would not.
Thus indeed no thanks is crowned about with words.

"O our Father, O King, highest of rulers, would that you might test this Job even to the end, and I would wish it, and it would be far more profitable, because by his own words he is an advocate of sinners."
He added rebellion to his grievous wickedness, knowing stubborn counsels, and he did not obey God's counsel;
And he clapped with his hands, and heaped reproaches on us, and with his own mind he spoke many disorderly words, foolishly, and not in order, to strive against God himself.
Thus he spoke;
And they all then were silent, nor did anyone dare to answer, for they knew well that they were harsh;
In silence they held themselves, and again he spoke a word;
Alas, did you, being good though you are, speak outrageously?
And you uttered a very arrogant word, as you declared, 'I for my part claim to be more righteous than God';
Do you think that you spoke this word according to what is right?
But let it be so, even if you said it: For what great benefit will there be, or what profit is there now for me, cleansed of my transgressions?
Or what does it avail me, since I have learned to be good?
Therefore, answering, I will pour forth a truthful voice, and I will speak plainly both to you and to your companions.
For one must speak out the word bluntly, both what I truly think and how I expect it to be accomplished.
Look up at the sky, which, high aloft above the earth, is spread out starry; and consider in your heart the clouds, which are borne far above you and hover in the air.
Of these there is one height; God's seat is forever secure; it is as far above as the sky is from the earth.
And what have you done to him that is beyond remedy, when you sin? Or in what many transgressions have you done it to him?
Or do you too, Job, yourself reap the fruit of your wickedness?
But even if you yourself give something in turn, what are you to your own people, O righteous one?
Or what profit is there for him?
Or what has he received from your hand?
Him neither the good man nor the bad man harms or benefits.
Your wickedness will soon reach the sons of Adam, such as you yourself are, and you will plant evil for men;
Your good order would avail mortal men, whether by word or by deed, bringing favor to humans.

Many arrogant and reckless men there are, who, yielding to violence, knowingly oppress the poor with their oath-breaking and force; from those being violated an unceasing groaning has arisen, and they are dragged off.
And still, while he acts violently, his mighty-working arm rages, which does not regard God.

Nor does anyone pass through these things, nor inquire, saying, 'Where is God who made me, who am nothing, and who appointed me, when I am to him toil and work, who gives a sweet song in the rainless night?'
Who teaches understanding to men, and manifold counsels, and gave to us to be more in mind than the beasts of the field and the birds of the air?
There both wailing and prayer of men arose together, while hubris was being destroyed, and on account of overweening ruin; but God sat silent, and like one who hears.
For neither does the heavenly Father, being kindly disposed, fix his mind on vain words, and on empty grief;
Nor did the Immortal ever hear the voice of an empty-minded man, when he regarded a man who might babble windy things.
Even if you said, 'I cannot yet see him face to face';
Easily and ever-knowingly does God prove himself, who is in his works, whose footprints are all-shining, and his beams are ever-jealous.
Beside him is justice, beside him is judgment, and also ordinances.
Therefore do you, taking courage, obey him greatly, and turn yourself back.
But now, since Job is not thus trusting in God, who has made him wretched, harsh, and miserable.
But that man, struck in his heart with great grief, did not know, nor did he understand what such a feast profits him, the wretch, which he holds according to fate by the will of God.
Therefore Job is a babbler and a man of measureless speech, from whose tongue indeed a most reckless utterance flowed.
He speaks many things exceedingly, but not with understanding.
Thus Elihu spoke;
and he answered him with a word, falling upon him:
Therefore speak again, and do not cease any longer from declaring;
Bear with me a little while, wait in silence, and I will recount to you the whole truth, since I still have more to say on God's behalf face to face.
Beginning from afar, uttering wise counsels, I will speak, revealing the ancient oracles of which we have learned;
I will set forth the ordinances of the heavenly King, and I will recount his justice and good order, who fitted me together skillfully, knowing well the crafts of building.
Shall I lie, or shall I speak the truth?
My heart urges me on.
For it is shameful for one who knows clearly to speak with lies.
Truly I will speak to you, and I will not weave falsehood.
And beside you is set one who has reached the summit of knowledge, who knows both the things that are, and the things that will be, and the things that were before.
God is mighty, and his strength is not feeble; but he has not neglected the lowly race of men, nor did he despise mortals though they be ever so weak.
Truly he is very mighty; who could match his fury?
So he is over all in life, and over noble minds, both a good king and a mighty warrior.
But of the sinners, whose cruel deeds are their care, he did not preserve their life, and he did not save the wicked, but they themselves perished by their own reckless follies.
For the wretched poor man he cares greatly, and he pities him, rendering justice well, and warding off heart-grieving outrage.

Never did he turn his gentle gaze away from the pious, and his eyes are always upon righteous men, and he set the upright on lofty thrones, so that they might obtain honor among mighty kings; there he established them continually, and they were raised up.
And if ever they were bound in collars and in fetters, and bonds of grievous toil were poured around them;
Meanwhile he revealed it to them, and wisely showed forth all the evils they had done in the follies of their mind, both their ruin and their grievous transgression.
And he opened their ears, and skillfully placed dense counsels in their hearts, so that they might not forget his commandments, but might keep their step turned back away from evil.
If thereafter they obey (since to obey is better), reverencing in their own hearts both his commandments and himself;
Then indeed they shall fill up their life, in much festivity, and with sweet joys as the years roll on;
But if they disobeyed utterly against his hateful-like decree, a sharp sword shall destroy them, and shall deprive them of dear life, and they shall perish ingloriously through follies of mind.
But those who devise deceit are helpless and worthless, and they spun wrath for the evil man unto his fated day;
For they do not even send up prayers to broad heaven, if ever the Immortal has laid a grievous bond upon them.
By this they are cut off beforehand, before they come to the threshold of old age; the ill-fated die, and their life wastes away swiftly amid the vile, in the midst of a crowd of fornicators.
But he delivered the poor man from affliction and misery, and in all his toils he stood by him and guarded him.
And he opened their ears, when violence and insolence came upon them.
So too would he have led you easily out of the narrow place into a broad room, and that which was set before you would have been full of fatness.
And you kept casting your hands upon the ready viands set before you, eating the goat's fly-defiled feast of the table.
But you eagerly accomplished the baneful counsels of the wicked; therefore I do not think you are safe, but now evil nemesis and fate overtake you.
Dreadful indeed is his wrath; so fear the anger of God, lest he strike you and take away your honey-sweet life.
For all that, you will not persuade him by bringing countless ransom.

Not even if you gave him ten times and twenty times as much, as much as ever was yours before, and even if other things came from somewhere; but not even so was his own heart ever going to consent, to release his dear soul, and to accept the ransom.
But all are to be rejected by God, his glorious gifts, as many as one might give eager to draw out his soul — in vain.
For he does not care for that, since he has no concern for wealth, nor indeed are so many talents of gold dear to him;
His strength and might count neither in word nor in number;
For he is exceedingly mighty, more than all men.
Do not yet long for the night, when peoples perish by some sudden fate together in their own land;
For no one can escape evil from God, nor through the night.
Consider, do not in your mind look upon worthless things, nor let transgression be a care to you in your heart, for you have chosen folly instead.
Easily and ever-known to God does strength become for men, those to whom he wished to grant surpassing glory.
Who could weave a counsel that wards off evil, as he himself does?
Who could match him as a teacher in knowledge?
Who guided his path for him like a escort?
And who taught him well, so that it might turn out far the best?
Or who will ever reproach him for his work, for all that he has done, contending against him, saying, 'Because you did not do this well'?
But you, never forget to marvel at his works, and to magnify them, which men always behold;
For they are manifest to all;
what mortal could fail to know them?
Easily indeed a willing man might survey them from afar, and nowhere does he gaze with dimmer eye from his head.
He is exceedingly great, and we still know him;
Such and as great as he was, alike good and great;
For God is hard for a mortal man to know;
His life is imperishable, but who knows the number of his years?
He poured down the finest gifts of finely-dropping dew, and watery drops to the earth;

But the air, thankless, after the moisture of the earth has fallen, sucks it back up again, fattening a fitting recompense, whenever it gives rain, a surplus equal to the vapor, pouring out the wetness which it had before drained from the ground.
The massy cloud is melted by the sun, and straightway it pours thick drops upon men, and a most violent water.

Who could understand the work of the cloud-gathering lord, with what kind of clouds he whirls the wide heaven around, how he spread out a cloud over the sky like a divine tapestry in his own tent, and great Olympus thundered?
At one time the sky was shadowy, and at another the clear air spreads out cloudless, and a bright gleam has run over it.
At another time with a dark cloud he covered the depths and roots of the sea, and the deep grew murky beneath it.

For often the Father is accustomed to punish humans with thick clouds for grievous transgression, on a summer day, when a great rainstorm with a wondrous squall comes upon them, and the works of humans diminish.
And often again he nourishes the life-giving grain with clouds.

As long as there are waterings through thick drops ever freshly coming from a hollow cloud, and they fly from heaven upon the spring flowers, and some swarm here in abundance, and others there, so long will great abundance of all fruits be about to come afterward, and the threshing floors weigh heavy greatly.
With purple clouds he wrapped Olympus around the body of the Sun, and he cast about it a shadowy mist, like a fine well-spun tunic, and drew it up into the light as the cloud went forth;
At this, both as the thunderbolt bursts and is destroyed, a dreadful crash arose, and the wide heaven bellowed;
And the cattle announce with a single-voiced cry the vapor, which they perceive rising up from the earth.
At these things my heart still beats within my breast, as I fear exceedingly, and my mind trembles within me;
And as when the West Wind, coming on, stirs the deep cornfield, rushing fiercely, and it nods with the ears of grain;
So my heart was stirred within me as I pondered.
But come, understand quickly the voice of God as he speaks; let his loud-bellowing, echoing sound fall upon you, which from his throat poured forth a much-resounding voice.

That one guided it straight under heaven, and taking the lightning in his hand he shook it from gleaming Olympus, and it, hurled by the swift-whirling stroke of God, ever flashing with dreadful gleams, flew.
Darting very swiftly through the upper air, straightway it reaches the boundless earth, and the tribes of men tremble.
Meanwhile a voice thunders from heaven, and beneath it the whole world crashed, and an unquenchable roar arose.

Then the High-Thunderer thundered greatly, and around him Olympus resounded terribly, and the boundless upper air bellowed, and the heavenly seat trumpeted, and the broad earth crashed, and beneath, the lord of the dead, Aidoneus, shuddered.
And the Father thundered terribly with a voice that breaks men, and having thundered he hurled a terrible bright lightning bolt, and a terrible crash arose from the flashing thunderbolt.
How great are the things he himself has done, which we cannot comprehend.
He who spoke to the snowstorm, 'Pour down upon the ground,' and soaked the earth, 'Go, rush forth, no longer stay idle in the clouds.'
So he spoke;
and the earth feared, and obeyed his word;
Straightway thick snowflakes fall to the ground, and like wool they are poured out upon the life-giving field, and there the earth is warmed, gleaming in its fleecy mantle.
And in like manner the Father commanded the rain and the storm, and they straightway pour forth, trembling at his rebuke.
There he put an end to toil, and checked the hands even of those eager for works, and there came a respite from labor;
So that wretched mortals may know well what he has done.
On that day the beasts lie down beneath the earth's hollows, and they couch in their hollow dens.
From the south, from the bright-shining one, a whirling storm arose, sending forth with a shrill blast a god-driven roar, lashing the dust-cloud with a hurricane about the paths;
And it, rushing down, stirs the violet-dark sea; and the great wave which it nourishes rolls on, and the foam is scattered aloft by the blast of the much-wandering wind.
Cold comes by the blast of the clear-sky-born North Wind, which ever smites the earth with chilling gales.
By the breath of God frost comes, icy-cold, and swiftly the wave of the fair-flowing river is frozen, being pressed together, and a smooth ice spreads over it.
It wears down the thick cloud with streams of water, and it was grieved as it was fed, and it is forced into the water-pregnant bosom.
And at another time again he scattered upon the much-nourishing earth the gleamings of the clouds, and the smoky missiles.

All these things are whirled about by the will of the great God, and on both sides the earth was rolled in an unceasing whirl, and the counsel which he enjoined upon them he fulfilled unerringly across the earth and across the world, and it obeyed his word.
Whether then he drives the impious with a mighty whip, or, gracious, pursues his much-burning land with rains, and warms the heart in the breasts of the pious.
Hear me, Job, and sit quietly a little while in amazement and silence, and lay up in your heart the wondrous marvels and dreadful works of God.
Do you know how God set the shadowy clouds, and again brought forth light from the scattered clouds?
Do you know indeed how the balanced clouds hang on high, weighed down by rains and waters?
What wonders he does — are his thoughts not sound, and his mind most high, knowing counsels about all things?

How were your garments overheated, and the earth was warmed, so that it slept gently away from the north wind and other scorching winds, except for the gentle south wind, to which God sent it to blow with a soft breeze?
Did you really stretch out the bright upper air along with him?
Or did you spread out the sky, all of bronze, above the earth, gleaming and firm, like a cast mirror?
But now you instruct us and grant us a word, for we do not yet clearly know how we shall answer him.
So great is the mist in our breasts.
Who then could show him my word?
if one should speak, like the flashing of a divine vision.
The light beneath the clouds — could a mortal behold it? — and the eye that darts keenest from the head does not see it.
But a rushing wind shook the shadowy clouds and blew with a clear-sounding whip, and cleansed the sky; and straightway it scattered the mist and drove off the fog.
And from it all the watchtowers appeared, and the lofty headlands, and the glens, and from heaven the boundless upper air burst forth.
Out of the north, brighter than gold, the cloudless sky is spread with fair weather; and the white calm came to the sea.
At this, beneath the blast, the boundless sky smiled with gleams; and all the earth around laughed, shining with radiance, and the flock rejoiced in heart.
How one dread glory belonged to the Most High, and to him both most radiant light and awful faces?
We cannot find out the nature of God who exists forever, even though we search with great eagerness and inquire;

He who was adorned with strength, and whose might is not to be assailed, who excels all in good order and in justice and in righteousness of mind, and never wished to vex a man overbearingly, as do the proud insolent men who wear others down by force, overstepping bounds.
Therefore mortals on earth tremble before him, reverencing the King, whose mind takes no pleasure in men, nor does he respect anyone who has shrewd counsels in his heart.
Thus he spoke bluntly;
and his companions stood speechless, marveling at the speech;
for very mightily he had spoken out.
But then God himself also spoke to Job out of the whirlwind, and he shook great Olympus;
Who is this that hides counsel by words without knowledge, foolish, and not knowing how to speak aright with his mind?
For he did not speak well;
so it seems to me he will recover his senses.
O blessed one, is it hard for you to draw out the counsels of the ever-living God, though you are very knowing?
But come now, take courage, and cast your belt about your waist; be a man, dear friend, and remember your furious valor.
Tell me, who am asking, the truth, and do not conceal it, since your spirit urged you to bring strife against God.
Tell me, if you understand, where were you when I laid the unshaken foundations of the rugged earth?
And who then set its boundaries?
Who measured it with a measuring-line (if indeed you know), and stretched it out upon a level, well and skillfully?
Or where were its balances hung, equal in weight, and it does not tilt this way and that?
How were its foundations fastened?
Who at the beginning laid its first stone, and rooted it beneath?
When the morning stars sang together with wondrous songs, which are the fairest stars in heaven?
And all the sons of God together shouted aloud exceedingly, rejoicing in joy, hymning their own father; and around them the great heaven trumpeted, and they echoed back.
Truly who shut in the resistless sea with doors, while it was yet an embryo, and from the subterranean hollows it gushed forth in a stream, and as from a womb it rushed out?
And a dreadful roar of the resounding sea, terrible, arose as the newborn one rushed forth?
Around it, as a cloak, they cast a cloud, and a tunic;
Dark-mantled mist was like a swaddling-band for it.
There gates and bars bound it, as I appointed before, and jutting headlands, strong defences, and around it the wave roared with rushing surge, and a smooth rock ran up;
And the water bubbled greatly, and the sea murmured;
Bound by a great shore, which indeed held even itself back, though it rushed eagerly in the foremost place.
For when I gave command, and rebuked and addressed you, "O Ocean, hold your fury — and why do you rage no longer bearably?"
Come now, going forth, much-resounding one, and see — do you not pierce through these bounds?
There hold your stream fast, and check your over-swollen waves;
But if I catch you overstepping this barrier with a bold wave, then this too shall be even worse for you.
So I spoke;
and he checked his stream, and held back his wave.
Was it you who once appointed the dawn, and commanded the twilight to know its place and likewise to keep its appointed hour?

And have you sent forth the saffron-robed dawn from heaven, so that it might shine upon the far-distant ends of the earth, so that by your wise directions the wicked, nameless, reckless men might quickly perish miserably headlong from the broad-wayed earth?

lg.l: "Ὄφρά κε τηλεδαποῖς ἐπιφώσκῃ πείρασι γαίης,
"Ὡς ἂν φραδμοσύνῃσι τεῇς ἀποφαινομενάων
"Ἀμπλακιῶν, νώνυμνοι ἀτάσθαλοι ἀνέρες αἶψα
Πρόχνυ κακῶς ἀπολοίατ' ἀπὸ χθονὸς εὐρυοδείης;

p.s: Or when it has stripped off the one black cloud of night, immediately it becomes all-manner of things, a great wonder to behold, smiling with all-varied hues and shapes;
with bright-gleaming forms, much-embroidered, like clay which a potter cunningly fashions with well-fitting front;
And the fair meadows laugh their fill, wearing a purple cloak and a flowery tunic.
There the insolence of men and baneful deeds are revealed.
For by my will the light has utterly perished from the impious, and the strong arm has been broken from the shoulder.
Have you ever gone down to the springs of the Ocean?
And the unsearchable depths and the watery foundations of the sea?
Or have you trodden the abyss of the sea and the boundless swell?
Were the gates of shadowy destruction opened for you?
And have you seen the misty portals of hateful night?
Or does the perishing shadow dwell in the hall of death?
But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly: do you know the breadth of the world, and does this concern you, to how far the circle has run round the wide earth?
And where does the light dwell?
Where are its people and its city?
Where does the darkness have its home?
And where is the chamber of the mist?
So that you may lead it home, having learned where its path is, if ever you might see it wandered away from its native land.
Do you really know these things well, since you are long-lived, and were born first of all, and know the most?
Have you ever seen the storehouses of snow with your eyes?
Or the treasures of much-resounding hail?
For hostile war these grievous missiles of mine lie always ready, with which I strike the heads of enemy men, and against whom I am angry on a baneful day.
Where then is the light divided under the starry heaven, and where does the broad-stretched east wind hasten?
Or whence, having come, is the sun's strength scattered abroad, when, raging with a wondrous storm, it has risen greatly from the unharvested ether?
Who has given channels to the rains and a course to the shower, and to the dread thunder, when it crashes from heaven, and to the solid thunder, and has driven a shining path?
So that it may wet the untrodden plain, and the grievous and desolate land, with abundant rain and blooming dew.

The earth, which before was thirsty and pathless, has now been satiated with the rich fruit-producing rain, so that in the spring season it may plant beautiful shoots, rejoicing with flowers of every kind.
Who is the father of rain?
Whose offspring does the rain know?
From whose womb and blood does it claim to be?
Or who has begotten the immortal drops of dew?
Who gave birth to the ice and nourished it, being such?
And who is its mother?
And from whose womb did the frost come forth, when the frosty night was, who gave birth to the cold hoarfrost?
As if with stone the waters were stopped up, and the stony streams stood frozen by the cold, and the hard surface was fixed fast; and then still the water rolls, well-closed, in its season.

Do you know clearly how to make the Pleiades rise, and the Hyades, and the late-setting Boötes, and the Bear, which they also called by the name Wagon, which turns itself and watches Orion, and all the other constellations with which the sky is crowned, each in its own season?
Can you bind the sweet-shining Pleiades as they rise with a rushing chain, or pour down as a sweet stream the rainy Hyades, or loose the strength of Orion, and the wintry bonds of sturdy Boötes?
Can you guide the zodiac signs well in the star-shining circle, and the old Arcturus with his sons, so that they, entering heaven, may fulfill their course according to due order?
Do you know the unwearying wheel of the aether, how the spheres are borne rolling around the pole?
And will he accomplish among earth-dwellers a gracious recompense of deeds unceasingly as the years roll round?
Are you then bronze-voiced?
Will you lift up your voice to the sky with a spear, as much as nine thousand or ten thousand bellow terribly, so that the many waters may cover you, Peploe, as the clouds melt from heaven?
Will you send a messenger to the earth, a blazing thunderbolt, saying, 'Go, speak'?
And did you hurl from the clouds the rushing lightning and fiery bolts?
Who put understanding in the breast, who placed the mind within?
Or who gave to the knowing mind the nature of oaks, and the works of living creatures?
Who knows the unspeakable number of the rain-bearing clouds?
Or who tilts the heavenly water-jars, pregnant with waters, so that they may not sprinkle the fields with ambrosial drops, when the fiery-bright pillar flashes?
When the earth was frozen fast, and the clods of the land were clotted, on the day when the most dust covered all around?
Will you hunt prey and booty for the mighty lions?
Will you appoint for them and their cubs a hunger-mingled feast?
And will you satisfy the craving of the cubs for drink and for food, while they lie hidden in a thick thicket, lurking in subterranean caves?

lg.l: Ὄφρα κατὰ κρύβδην κέαται πυκινῇ ἐνὶ λόχμῃ
Σίνται, ὑποχθονίοις ἄντροις ἔνι φωλεύοντες;

p.s: Who has prepared a meal for the ravens that lack it, when through the meadow the nestlings, helpless young, wander to and fro for want of food, and call upon God, sending forth a harsh cry?
Do you know when the wild rock-goats give birth?
Or when the race of fawn-bearing does are in labor?
Do you know the number of the months which they fulfill, being pregnant, bearing every month, and do you know the season of their bringing forth?
They crouch down and give birth, bringing forth their dear young; and the sharp shaft of the birth-pangs' Eileithyia holds them, both Fear and mighty Terror, bringing on bitter pangs.

Their children are well-fed and fully satisfied with food, and growing easily they shine with sleek limbs, and gently from their bed they creep on tiny feet, and when by grievous childishness they have wandered away from their parents, they no longer remember to urge their step back home.
Who set the wild ass free, unmastered, having loosed its bonds—the swift one, storm-footed, strong-hoofed, the steep-dwelling wild ass?
For him I made a home in a desert land, and he dwelt alone upon the barren earth.
Far from the crowd the city-hater straightway wanders, shunning the people, and he has fled the great din of the throng, nor ever did he heed the mighty threat of a violent master, a shepherd's;
nor does he pay heed to the shout, nor to the driver.
In the glens of the mountain he ever wanders seeking the newly-sprouted grass, and from the green herbage he had his pasture; the all-nurturing earth feeds him to satiety.
Fool, do you think that you can tame the wild unicorn, so that it might be your own exceedingly great possession, and your own, eating white barley like an ox at the manger?
Or, like an ox, will you put a halter on it along the furrow under the yoke, to draw, so that it might cut the straight furrow in the broad fallow land, and the clod might yield under the plough?
In this, then, do you trust in its strength, because its power is pre-eminent?
Because you are strong, will you entrust your works to him?
Do you say that he will carry off the fruit of your perfect harvest?
And to bring it home, as the year rolls round, (is it the way of slaves, and of straight-horned oxen) to thresh it well in a well-built threshing floor?
Did you give beautiful broad-feathered wings and shining plumage to the straight-rumped, long-winged peacocks?
With which, exulting in their wings and in their own beauty, they overshadow the whole body with a circling, dappled form, sprinkled with thick eyes here and there, a wonder to behold;
Do you give wings and feathers to the ostrich?
But when she has laid a single egg, she leaves it on the ground, and does not warm her offspring, covering it round with her dear wings, as is the custom for birds;
But these are warmed in the soft dust by the rays and are stolen away by the sun.
Foolish one, she does not know this in her mind, nor did she understand when the wild beasts, meeting her, would have seized her as a hapless bed, and would have dashed her down under their feet.
A mother, a cruel mother, and having a harsh spirit, who as it were is bereft of her children, so that she does not know her offspring.
her heart is iron indeed.
Because when she had in vain, just so, escaped the mighty pangs of grievous childbirth, the cruel one neglected her young, nor did she spare them lest they suffer anything.
For God did not give her understanding in her breast, nor did he allot her skill, and he did not grant her good wits.

Or when she flutters in the air and in the clouds, as is the custom of other birds that soar aloft, and lifts her shaggy head and breast on high, as it were equal, spreading her wings like sails and canvas, she runs swiftly over the land with the blasts of the wind, like some self-moving ship on foot, for which alone, renowned for their deeds, there are steersmen behind.
And having driven alongside, she laughs alike at horseman and horse, swifter than both to run, and greater than the one in pursuit.
Is it truly you who gave strength to the warlike, valiant horse, swift, bronze-hoofed, strong-clawed, dark-maned?

Around him it bristles a shaggy neck with thunder; and his breast is massive, his frame long, his back broad, his tail curved like a scorpion's; and he darts exulting through the plain, and holds his head on high, and around his shoulders the manes stream, and he, trusting in his splendor, swiftly bears himself along, and far off his hairs are terrible.

Do you really terrify it like a cicada, which, sitting on a tree throughout the wood, sends forth its lily-like voice, and whenever it sees any one coming, or hears a noise, it is terribly frightened, and pale fear seizes it?
It remembers flight, and forgets its lively song.
How do you stir up fear and terror in its breast?

But he, snorting, snorts up a great blast; with his feet he has dug out the glens for the horses, trusting in his strength; marching over the plain he has met a dense phalanx, dread, bristling with shields and spears; and he rushes to mingle in the baneful battle as quickly as possible.

lg.l: Πλιῶσιν ἄγκεα ποσσὶν ὀρώρυχεν ἀλκὶ πεποιθώς,
Καππεδίον στιχόων πυκινῆς ἤντησε φάλαγγος,
Δεινὸν τῷ σάκεσίν τε καὶ ἔγχεσι πεφρικυίης,
Ἀρξεῖται δ' τάχιστα μιγήμεναι ἐν δαῒ λυγρῇ.

p.s: Nor then does fear hold him, harmless as he is, nor does he tremble overmuch, as soon as he has settled himself against a band of men.
For neither can he, as he shies away, fight with a naked foe, nor strike, nor watch for the bridges of war, beneath the flash of bronze and the gleam of the sword.
Terribly, right before them, he glares with unblinking eye upon the warriors, at the ambush thickly set with spearmen, and at the gleaming bronze and the flashing iron.

And he went through the front ranks; then indeed, facing him, the bow twanged, the quiver rattled, and the arrow rang out; and around his shoulders the all-shining armor crashed, and the gleam reached heaven, and the phalanxes were stirred; and they stood there massed against him, close-fighters, having thrust spear against spear, shield against shield set layer on layer.
But he went among the foremost, exulting in his strength; and his eyes blazed fiercely beneath his scowling brows, flashing like the gleam of burning fire, and foam came about his mouth as he fought.
With his feet he has been roused to wage war, where he snorts in the dust, and with his nostrils he gulps down the ground.
And his chest was stirred, and his mane tossed on high, and beneath his armor a dust-storm rose rushing.

But whenever the trumpet, herald of war, cried out, and the warlike pipe sent forth its battle-stirring voice, then he pawed the ground, longing for war, and was roused standing upright, and did not stand still on his feet, and at the clear sound of the trumpet rushing on, he says he hears it, for fierce madness has entered him.
Amid the trumpets he neighs very greatly, terrible, exulting;
And he exults in his heart with joy, smelling the battle-cry and the fray from afar, the thunder of leaders and the war-shout of those fighting.
By your wisdom does the swift-winged hawk rise to fly, the kestrel, when it brings slaughter to the little birds, and flutters toward the south exulting in its wings?
And at your command the great eagle, the high-flyer, cleaves the sky, which is preeminent among all birds, and high in the clouds it has fixed its shameless nest?
He dwells on a jutting rock and a misty crag, on a lofty, great one, and he abides on a cleft rock, on a steep, sturdy one, where his home and shelter are.

There no sea-watching lookout sits, nor from expectation does he peer in every direction, if perhaps he might catch a great prey; but from afar from a lookout he saw a corpse with his keen eye, for he gazes sharpest of the birds above.
His flesh-eating young he fed with glistening fat, and they have always consorted with the dead.

So spoke the holy might of the Immortal unrelentingly; nor did he cease from words any longer, but again he spoke a speech, and again he answered Job, and rebuked him and addressed him: 'Who now would dare to strive against God face to face, and to lay before him counsel and understanding of mind?'
He will repay threefold and fourfold, whoever would dare to reprove him.
For it is grievous to contend against the Olympian.
And the children of the wretched will meet my word.
So he spoke.
But glorious much-enduring Job shuddered, and stood silent before God, and a dread terrible fear came upon him.
And at last he addressed him, and spoke a God-persuaded word:
Woe is me, wretched, and the most refutable of the living!
Shall I myself open my foolish mouth against the Immortal?
It is not possible, nor is it fitting for you, Father, to speak in reply;
Therefore I wish to press my hand upon my mouth.
Truly I spoke once, and a second time again I spoke;
But no longer did my spirit in my breast dare to speak a second time in reply, but it urged me to sit in silence, still, since it is far better so.
Then God, answering him, spoke with a sweet voice out of the midst of the whirlwind; broad heaven trembled beneath him, he shook upon his throne, and he made great Olympus quake.
O good sir, be a man; gird your loins about your waist; take courage, and do not be at all greatly afraid in your heart; tell me truly when I ask, and do not conceal it.
O sir, will you really now make my counsels vain idle things?
But do you really think my sharp mind and purpose cannot pass by a cowardly mortal, nor catch him out?
Will you indeed justify yourself, judging against me?
Is your arm indeed, like God's, stretched out great?
Who is it that also, having brandished about a fiery thunderbolt,
and thundered terribly from the sky, like that one, with a loud-roaring voice?
and having brandished lightning together with your hand?

But come now, if you can match my strength, then shine, clothed in divine might of splendor, gleaming with beauty and graces and flashes, smiling with grim countenances, and cast glory about you, and clothe yourself with wondrous light upon your face.
Scatter your wrath, your sharp anger, your indignation, and your ruin over all the earth;
wherever you saw proud men, cast them down, and there especially direct your avenging eye;
Strike them, looking askance, so that each falls to the ground, men overweening and tongueless, whoever they are;
From their seats drag down the wicked, so that they too, prone in the dust, may bite the earth with their teeth.
Trample with your heel upon their breasts, and beneath their feet hide them together in the dust, the wicked tribes of mortals who overflow with pride;
Bind them head-down, and let darkness cover their eyes.
Meanwhile I will gladly yield, nor will I refuse, since your right hand has granted you a mightier boast.

But now behold the monstrous elephant, mighty-limbed; truly it was fashioned a great marvel, and it is not like a mountain-dwelling beast, but like a wooded mountain-height of lofty peaks, or even a shadowy cloud.
Him too he made along with you, so that he might eat the fruit of the field.
For he is not a robber among the beasts, nor any devourer, though he be such and so great in body, but ever he grazes in the green and rich pastures, like a herd ox in an asphodel meadow.
Irresistible strength and might attend his flanks; in his lowest belly and navel there is power.
Its tail is indeed like a cedar, and he whirled it about very swiftly with ease;
His testicles are bound with well-woven joints, and they are drawn tight with sinews and twisted cords and fibres.
His skin resembles bronze, and his body gleaming iron; his ribs and limbs are fitted with stout bones, as with bronze bolts and iron bars.
And among the works of God he boasts that he is greatly pre-eminent, and among the wild beasts he is by far the mightiest;
He who indeed fashioned him armed him, as it were with a sword, with a great snout, both twisted and crooked;
They used to call it a proboscis.

But he is not flesh-eating, nor wild, nor blood-stained; but the mountains have abundantly given him fodder, where all the beasts leap together facing him, and no one is afraid of him nor fears him, when he sees an elephant.
Trees give him cover with their high foliage, a shady forest; there the reeds and the marsh lie hidden in a dense thicket, and in the watery meadow of a great marsh.

Beside the roaring river, around the rustling reed-bed, there deep-shaded tall trees tend him, poplars and elms and willows that lose their fruit, which grow abundantly around the fair streams of the river.

Often a river has drunk it down, gulping with insatiable [throat], and has ravaged the stream — the sheer torrents of the Jordan — he boasts that he will easily, very easily, gulp them with his sturdy jaws.
Who could subdue this one with well-woven nets, and capture him openly, and pierce through his nostril with a hook?
But I will tell you another wild wonder, a sacred [creature] of fishes, a mighty sea-monster of the deep, a great marvel of the sea;
(For not only the land breeds monsters, but the sea too)
Can you draw him out of the sea with a line, and with gleaming bronze, and put a hook around his tongue?
Can you pierce his nose, so full of gulfs, with curved hooks, and fix a great spike around his jaws?
But will he, being appeased, charm you with vows and gentle supplications?
And will he vow to you to be a suppliant, speaking with soft and wheedling words?
Will he indeed, bringing you favors, give soothing charms to your heart?
Will he make a covenant, cutting oaths, so that after catching him alive you may hold him in a servant's lot?
Will you really make him a plaything for infants?
Will you tie him up like a bird, sweetly, with a shining cord, and give him to maidens, so that you might be a plaything for them?
Will your loving comrades devour him at a feast, and will they carve a glorious banquet from his flesh?
Or, since he is great, will they cut him limb from limb and send him to the fishmongers, one place and another, who in turn will sell him and take a vast price?
Will you pierce all around the hide of the dread monster with sharp javelins and with two-edged spears?
Or will you wound his flesh with jagged-toothed, many-barbed iron, and his head with far-barbed tridents?
But come, with your own hands lay hold of his back with a mattock, since with gentle force you would only subdue him alone;
Give way, and do not remember the battle, but cease from your rush.

If anyone wishes to lay him low by guile or by force, yet he fails utterly, and his hope is lost; for the beast is a grievous evil for a man to subdue, dreadful, grim-eyed, implacable, nor would anyone rejoice to see him, so great is he to look upon.
Is there no one with such a heart in his own breast as to rouse him, whoever is so bold-hearted?
and boldest of all;
who of me, who could endure to stand Antion before him with a great-hearted spirit?

Who, having come first, gave me a fitting answer, so that I too, (truly, as is right,) might repay him a twofold, gracious recompense for what he has done, and that he might receive from me a heart-pleasing wage?
For all things are mine, all that heaven has encompassed.

But still I will tell you of the great sea-monster, the wonder of the sea, and I will not hide it from you, nor yet the tale — how its limbs, how its mighty frame, how its growth, how its wondrous form.
Who dragged it from the sea to the dry shore of the mainland, and showed its dread form in its scaly coat?
And who, having put his hand upon it, casts a double bridle around it?
Who has fixed stakes in its curved jaws, and in its gullet?

And its gates were opened like double-folding doors, and they were lofty; and its dreadful jaws bellowed with a terrible gaping, and fearsome teeth stood round about on both sides, close-packed and crowded, more numerous than black death.
He exults in his bronze scales, firmly rounded, like the engravings of a well-fitted seal.
And these are poured close upon one another, so that not even the finest air can slip in between.
As when a man fits a wall with close-set stones of a lofty house, shunning the violence of the winds;
As then helmets and bossed shields were fitted together, so that in war the close-packed ranks were thrown into confusion, shield pressed on shield, helm on helm, or tortoise-shell on Arthēn;
as on it the scales were fitted around its bronze back, each to the other, and neighbor pressed on neighbor, so closely are they grown together in unbroken union.
And when from his nostrils a deep-roaring snorting was burst forth, fire blazed, and a terrible flash of flame appeared, and his eyes that flashed like the dawn were like them in his eyelids.
From his mouth torches and unquenchable flame were poured forth in vain, and from it many sparks leaped out.
As when smoke flows from a tripod or a cauldron, which seethes greatly within, urged on by the soothing fire, melting with fat, and quickly its blast reaches heaven;
Thus from his nostrils smoke flows as he breathes terribly.
Into his mouth and nostrils a fire-breathing furnace leaps, and flame gushes around, and a swift torch is kindled.
His strength is in his neck, and his might is not feeble; and around his sturdy neck boundless valor settles.
A great joy comes to them all at once, but grief to sailors.

He delights, treading upon the back of the sea, where, eager to sport in the grim storm, he leaps over the purple wave, and frisks in the midst of the wine-dark deep, exulting just so, even if he is ill-tempered.
The folds of his flesh are unbroken and unloosed around his limbs, and his frame is well fitted together, and a firm belly has risen up over his mighty breast, all of bronze, ever secure.
And his heart is firmer than stone, like an unyielding millstone, and his mind is dark all around.
And he was like a tower above the sea.

But when he rose up, a dreadful one appeared; at once the sailors trembled in their heart, terrified, for they are borne but a little away from death, mighty though they be, when they saw the mighty fish; and they cleansed themselves, when the salt water cut them, and the monstrous sea-monster broke through the nourishing waves.
If anyone struck him in the body with a sword, he did not notice, nor did he break his hide.
and the point was bent back.
Or he hurled a missile, and it fled from his hand in vain.
Bronze spears, long lances, shafts, and javelins were dashed against his skin, and the bronze blade was driven off from the bronze.
He thinks the blazing iron is like a reed, and unyielding bronze is like a dry stick of wood.
He does not flee, nor is he frightened by the feathered arrow.
Like chaff that is on well-rolled threshing floors, which the wind and the rush of the winnower carry away.
As stones which they seem to be, which a man hurled with a sling, shooting them; and his onset seemed to him vain.
As he, going on, pays no heed to javelins, and he thinks them equal to chaff, or to be air; and as from a ship the might of the wind scattered them.
But if someone, brandishing it, hurls a long-shadowed spear, yet he, laughing aloud, would mock the man's rush, paying no heed, as if a woman or a foolish child should strike him.

Beneath him sharp crags are fixed, and around him rocks and cliffs and jagged pointed stones, which he pierced above the mire, like a bed in the broad sea, on which the great one lay stretched out mightily.
And as when water seethes in the midst of gleaming bronze, boiling up from every side, and beneath it lie the dry crackling sticks;
And the fire busied itself about the cauldron, and the water grew hot;
as a cauldron;
it boils within, hastened by much fire, and bubbling with myrrh and nine-year-old ointment;

As the wave of the much-resounding sea, churned up, seethed on high for the swimmer, and the deep foamed, roaring with foam, and the salt water bubbled up, and it swelled aloft, and the wild swell of the sea boiled.

And he goes, but behind him a great shining abyss; for him even as he breaks it roars greatly, and around his own curved wave with its crest, and he spits out the foam of the sea, and to Apheidea appears the path of the grey sea; you would say you were looking at the head of a grey-templed old man, or a milk-white circle even in the waters.
In no way did any beast upon the much-nurturing earth come to completion, nor in the depths of the sea, to be likened to him — neither in body, nor in nature, nor in might, nor in any form.
So was his heart in his breast bold and fearless.
Exulting greatly in strength and might he sprang up, and he kept gazing at all things lofty, and among the proud he boasted that he was a king, and greatly pre-eminent among monsters.
Then much-enduring noble Job answered him, bending his heart back, and spoke a God-persuading word:
I know that you are mighty, and you can accomplish all things, (for your wonders are everywhere over dry land and sea) and no one among mortals has frustrated your purpose.
Who is this that hides counsel with ignorance of mind, foolish (as you said) and not knowing things aright in his thoughts?

I erred myself, and I did not speak according to what is right — many years and even so; and disease and those things commanded it, and painful folly, things which I did not see nor understand, many unspeakable wonders.
For you are a God of crooked counsel; nor could any mortal draw back your gifts.
But, O Lord, have mercy, and if any dreadful word has been spoken, let the storm-winds snatch it up and carry it off at once.

I know you, Father; do you also give heed and listen to me, and now recount to me the whole truth, and teach me your close counsels, that I may learn; and be to me a speaker of words and a reckoner of deeds.
I used to hear of you in time past, and I listened with the ears of report; but now my eye has seen you face to face.
Know that you are noble and divine;
awe holds me as I look upon you.
Therefore I loathed myself, being foolish, seeing what I have done, like a fool, since I am the most shameful among men.

But since I erred, trusting in wretched thoughts, therefore, wrapped in dust and in ashes, rolling over and over, I now come to you and to your knees, grieving as I weep, and I am greatly distressed, at how I erred.
Woe is me, wretched that I am!
But do you put on a gracious heart.
So he spoke, shedding tears.
And a whirlwind seized the Almighty King.

But when they were speaking such things to one another, God, having grown angry, addressed Eliphaz the Temanite (for he was indignant at the divine man), and kept rebuking him with a word: "Alas, surely I am exceedingly angry with you and your companions, and wrath has fallen upon my spirit."
Wretched men, you have spoken like foolish children, who have no understanding in their minds.
You have not spoken rightly about me, as my servant Job has.
Whenever a man wishes to strive with the Deity on behalf of a mortal, one whom God honors, swiftly a great calamity rolls upon him.
But you too, be persuaded, since to obey is better, and take from the herd seven oxen, rolling-footed, curved-horned, as fast as possible, and seven rams, thick-fleeced.

And go now to Job, so that on account of your folly you may perform noble sacrifices upon much-lamented altars, and my servant Job may pray duly, if perhaps he may be gracious to you and himself give acceptable gifts always to me; and now I know that he will give.
Him I loved with all my heart, and he honors me, preeminent above others.
For whoever obeys me, I have heard him well.
Otherwise again I think that you will soon have your fill, because your minds are not steadfast, nor according to what is right, as my servant Job — you have spoken about me.
So he spoke;
and Eliphaz the Temanite did not disobey God, nor did Bildad the Shuhite, nor Zophar the Minaean;
But they sacrificed and, with abundant offerings and savory fat, turning him aside, they soothed the wrath of the Immortal;
Then indeed Job prayed to God — to God he prayed — and he heard his prayers, and loved him more, and granted him favor.
Thus he prayed on behalf of his friends;
And God loosed the bonds of his dread misery, and granted him twice as much wealth as he had before, and gave him other things from elsewhere.

All his brothers came of their own accord in a throng, and all his own sisters, and kinsmen by marriage, and clansmen; and those who had been his most honored and dearest before stood by him always at feasts and banquets in his own halls, and with consolations they soothed his mind, and with winning words they healed his grief, and comforted him, and lamented what he had suffered, and how he had toiled in misery by the will of God — (such a thing some other mortal on earth endured) — and they gave him a necklace of silver and gold, glowing gifts, a comfort for his evil ruin.
So then Job was more blessed than before, twice as wealthy and twice as happy-fated, as much as he had at first, by the will of the great God.

For indeed he had afterward twice seven thousand sheep, fat and thick-fleeced, and high-crested camels twice four thousand grazing for him in the mountains, females with young (and all these had been made double), and twice fifty yoke of broad-browed oxen, and twice fifty donkeys, and all things far more abundant.
But also his ten children were in the halls;
Seven were sons, and three fair-haired daughters.
Of these, the one was called by the famous name Jemimah, the First, because the night of misery had passed, and day had come;
And after her the younger was Kassia, lovely — Kassia, a beautiful name, whose fragrance was most gracious;
And the third they called fair-tressed Keren-Happuch, because he gave her a splendid horn of antimony as a name.
And adorned with beauty and with graces they shone among women, and easily stood out among the field-faring folk.
Nor would any of the neighboring maidens have wished to contend with Job's daughters in lovely beauty;
To them their father assigned a portion together with their brothers, apportioning it, and gave countless dowries.
But Job thereafter, alive and sound, saw a hundred and forty years rolling by in great splendor, and children still flourishing on both sides, and children of children, down to four generations.
Thus then he gladly reached the end of his life, dying late, and caught in the extreme of old age.
